utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I remind you the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told that on the evening of the 20th you returned to Negoslavci and you told Vojnovic about what had occurred. I want to move on, if I may, to subsequent events. Are you able to remember when it was or indeed if you heard of any reports circulating in the area about possible atrocities occurring at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that several times there were already the first comments on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you at any time aware of an investigation occurring immediately thereafter, an investigation into what had occurred at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the security organs from Sid about the rumours about atrocity having been committed and they suggested that we should not be dealing with that problem, that this will be done by other people who were out in the field and that I should really deal with the security matters pertaining to my duties as part of the 80th regular Brigade. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic. Oh, Mr. Domazet. Could I remind counsel to be conscious of time. I don't put it higher than that, because I recognise that at least in some cases this witness is of significance. But there are significant time constraints put on the availability of the witness to us by the government of Serbia, and the witness must return to Serbia after today. Therefore, I leave you with that thought, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukosavljevic, good morning. I am Vladimir Domazet, and I represent Mr. Mrksic. Mr. Vukosavljevic, first of all, a few things from your CV, which was already covered by my learned friend Mr. Moore. And as pertaining to your career as a reserve officer, it wasn't quite clear in your movements in your CV whether you worked until the time you completed your university education, which was sometime in 1984 when you were already 30 something, 37 years old.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was about 35, 36 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After completing high school, did you work somewhere before you graduated in 1984?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to broaden a little bit my answer to your question so that we don't have to discuss that again. I worked -- I completed the secondary mechanical school in 1966, then I worked in a factory for special manufacture, and then I completed the higher engineering school, so I was an engineer of the -- at sixth level. After I completed that, I moved again to the car manufacturing factory as part of Zastava. I worked there until 1977. Then I went back to my birth place and I worked in an enterprise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and then I started to work in 1977 or 1978, and then I graduated at the faculty of organisational sciences in 1984, so by that time I already had quite a few years of work experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you went to Zastava in 1972 when you were about 25 years old. At the time, the compulsory military service was 18 months?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For people who had completed higher education or university education, it was 12 months, but for those who had high school education, it was 18 months. I served 11 months because I was released earlier because of my good grades in school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that you served 12 months because you were in the reserve officer's school? So my question is all those who went to the reserve officer's school, regardless of the level of their education, served their military duty for 12 months and not for 18 months; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not think you are right because the military term then was 15 and 12 months, those who had completed secondary education, regardless of whether they attended the reserve officers schools. But let me tell you, this is something that I recall from 30 years ago, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time, in order to go to the reserve officers school, am I right if I say that it was necessary in your CV for it not only to be clean in terms of prior convictions or prosecution, but you also had to be politically vetted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I agree with what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This also applies even more so to those who, like you, later attended the security schools or worked in the duties that you worked in as a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't want to comment on that, because the election of cadres to certain posts is an official secret and I do not have the authorisation of the government to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time when you served in the military and when you attended the reserve officers school in our country, there was the so-called single-party system. There was only one party, the League of Communists. Were you a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, but I must remind you that, besides that, there was also the Socialist Alliance of the Working People, so that was also a party, so it wasn't just the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, let's not discuss that. As you say, members of the Socialist Alliance were all the of-age citizens of the country, so we're not going to go into that in particular.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of them, but the majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, let's move on. You explained your advancement as a reserve officer, and then finally in 1990 or 1991 you became the chief of the security organ in the 80th Motorised Kragujevac Brigade. Can you tell me, briefly, your role as the chief during this attempt to carry out a mobilisation in 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a general answer. In principle, I tried to carry out all the mobilisations in the best possible way, to make sure that unit was fully mobilised. Which is the chief of security's job anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you were doing that work even before you went to Negoslavci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time, did you already know the other officers and soldiers from the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main work of the security organ is based on knowing your people, from soldiers up to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So can I conclude that you knew well both the soldiers and the officers in the brigade, that you were the chief of security before you left for Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can conclude that, because that was the nature of my personal or official assessment, but of course you cannot know anyone completely. There are always possible surprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm going ask you about Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Did you know him at the time, did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic, at the time Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, was a person I got to know during the second call-up because the brigade commander was replaced after the first call-up, and Mr. Vojnovic came in his place. So I met him. He had come from Slovenia, so I didn't know him for as long as I knew some of the other officers and soldiers in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were talking about mobilisation and going to Smederevo and then to Negoslavci, when we're talking about the military police, you also said that your brigade had two platoons of the military police, and one platoon of traffic police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, another service detachment, which was a very expert unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One of those platoons was resubordinated to another unit, or let's put it more simply, didn't go with you to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can say that it was taken out of the military police unit of the 80th Motorised and attached to another military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me where it was attached to, and where did it go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left, actually when this military police platoon was taken out of the 80th Motorised Brigade, I didn't know from the superior command where that platoon would be sent. However, later I found out that it was part of a battalion from the Belgrade Military District, and that they were advancing from the Sotin village, Bulgarian cemetery, Mitnica village axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In any case, you did not have any contact with that platoon in the course of the operations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was returned sometime on the 24th or the 25th, but I'm not sure about the date. That was when it returned to the units, but based on the unit documents, you can find this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to the part when you arrived at Negoslavci with your brigade, and I assume that you formed a command. So were you, as the security organ, located at the same place as the command and your Commander Vojnovic, or were you at a different location?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to avoid any additional questions, let me tell you that the command of the 80th Brigade was billeted in the three houses at the end of the village of Negoslavci. Different organs were deployed in those three houses. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic had his command post in a vehicle, a TAM vehicle, and he was there with his signalsmen. I wasn't there with him, I was next door to him, and we could access each other very quickly and we cooperated very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something else: Yesterday to my learned friend's question you spoke very briefly about the organisation of your security organ in the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I talk about the number and deployment of the security organ in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Precisely. I would like you to talk about your subordinates, because you were the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it very clearly yesterday, and my answer today cannot differ much from my answer yesterday. At the level of the brigade, I was the chief of the security organ, and I had two subordinated officers. One was an officer and the other one was a non-commissioned officer. In the 1st, the 2nd and 3rd Battalions the security organs were at the same time organs for intelligence and counter-intelligence, and in the rear battalion I had a security organ who was just a security organ and he did not have the intelligence role. I had two people directly subordinated to me, and the security organs in the battalions were directly linked to the commanders. They informed me about the events in their respective units along the lines of our common profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this also apply to the security organs in the units resubordinated to your 80th Motorised Brigade; for example, the 185th tactical unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether -- which number did you say, excuse me? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: 195th tactical group.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about the things that I am familiar with. We had an uncomplete brigade from Croatia that joined our brigade. They had a lot of technical equipment, but very few men. And in that brigade there was just an officer in charge of security. He was an Albanian. He reported to me and I helped him -- I asked him to assess the security of his brigade. He didn't use that. He had been married to a Slovenian, he returned to Slovenia, he abandoned his brigade, and that brigade no longer had a security organ and that brigade was very soon taken out from the strength of the 80th Motorised Brigade, so I didn't have any contact with them and I didn't have to work with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well then. This is as far as the security line is concerned, and those who were subordinated to you and who reported to you or to whom you gave tasks. At the moment when you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please comment upon the question of the Defence counsel? Because the question was not put in appropriately. I had two immediately subordinated officers, and the others, those who were in the battalions, were not directly subordinated to me. They were subordinated to their respective commanders. We cooperated along the lines of our profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is what I'm talking about; the security line, the professional line, not the chain of command, which is completely clear to all of us. I'm talking about the line of the security organ that is very special in its work. And if we're talking about that line, I would like to know when you arrived in Negoslavci and when you were involved in the Operation Vukovar. Who was it who gave you instructions, orders, along that line? Who did you cooperate with directly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor's question, I already spoke about that, and I informed the Trial Chamber about that. Around the 10th the brigade command told me that the brigade command was subordinated to the Guards Motorised Brigade; in other words, that the Guards Motorised Brigade is also the command of the OG South, and according to the rules of service, a subordinated security organ has to report to his superior security organ in the command. I went to the command post of the Guards Motorised Brigade and in -- and I found Captain First Class Karan with whom I had the initial conversation that concerned our profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is whether you reported to him like those who were subordinated to you reported to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is a uniformity in reporting in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If there was a role that Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic played at the time, the person who came from Kragujevac, what was his role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic from the counter-intelligence group of the 24th Corps, he was the assistant chief of security of the 24th Corps for the police work. He was in charge of the work of the military police battalion and all the police units in the 25th Corps [as interpreted], those that were subordinated to the 25th Corps [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where were his located physically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was physically located in the corps command in Kragujevac. I can't give you the exact number, but I am going to tell you that on several occasions he came to Vukovar. I would say that he came to control and to assist us with some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before I ask you another question, I would like to make a correction in the transcript. I asked you, and you said that this was the 24th Corps, and a mistake has been made, and the corps mentioned here is 25th instead of 24th. So if I have understood you well, Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic was located in Kragujevac, but he would come from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a certain other number of officers from the counter-intelligence group from Kragujevac, they would come to Vukovar to visit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what was their role, his role and those who came with him, with respect to you and your brigade and your work as a security organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their work consisted of several things. They provided me with instructions, they helped me with certain tasks, but by and large we were colleagues. They would come and help me out on the ground with anything that I was involved in on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the work of the officers who were involved in counter-intelligence in the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise; can you be more specific? Can you clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is who was in charge of the work of the officers who were involved in counter-intelligence in the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professionally, it was me. I'm talking about the two officers who were my subordinates, so I was the one they reported to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a plan of counter-intelligence measures or an excerpt of -- from such a plan? I suppose you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can be very open about that. Those are two documents which are not an official secret of the security organ. The security organ, i.e., the subordinated command, receives from its superior command all the orders concerning security, specifying all the security measures that have to be applied in the subordinated unit, and this is something that there is no two ways about. You receive a document entitled a document on security, it arrives at my address and informs me about the security situation in my brigade, in the neighbouring brigades, in the command. Those are public documents and there is nothing that we cannot discuss with regard to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you often use the term "official secret" and you are obviously bound by a secret, if we ever come to something that might be a secret, could you please advise us. Maybe you will be able to answer such a question if we move into private session. If not, and you have called upon some rules, the rules of your service, and according to those rules there is such a thing as official secrets, however everything is used in this Tribunal as evidence, we kindly ask you to provide us with as much detail as possible. You have mentioned a decision, can you please tell us briefly what this is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my government's decision here. Maybe I should read it to you, or maybe it could be placed on the ELMO, but I can read it out to you so as to show you what this is all about and what my government has asked me to do and what not to do. "Pursuant to Article 11 of the Cooperation between Serbia and Montenegro with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia --" I apologise. "Pursuant to Article 11 of the Law on Cooperation between Serbia and Montenegro and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the Official Gazette of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, 18/2002 and the Official Gazette of Montenegro, the Council of Ministers hereby issues the following decision --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast. We cannot follow this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long is this document? Two pages. Mr. Domazet, I'm not sure what is the point of this document being read. If you have a specific question, put it to the witness. If he says he can't answer it because of that document, then we can deal with that issue. But we don't need to know the details. This is, in my experience, a standard document from the Serbia and Montenegrin government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is a standard document myself, and that in these proceedings there is no such secret that the witness could not talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You don't have to proceed. If we ever come across a problem, we -- I hope we will be able to resolve it. When you were talking yesterday about your relationship with your superiors along the line of security, you said that your impression was that there was a lack of interest among your superiors in you and your work. Did it also -- were you saying that you were therefore sent to Karanfilov as the second in command rather than commander himself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This period of cooperation did not last long enough for me to have any more serious intentions. I said that the chief of security of the 80th Brigade, Colonel Sljivancanin [as interpreted], was very correct towards me. Everybody else was also polite. But truth be told, the strength of my brigade was not such as to be interesting for the superior command. We had very few men. We only had two and a half independent companies and a headquarters command, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your earlier statements and yesterday, you spoke about the reports that you wrote. You said that you wrote these reports in three copies and that you kept one copy for yourself. Did you send one copy to the superior command and did this apply to only this period, or also the later period when you were linked to the command in Sid?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was about the time when I was linked to the command in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript it says that you were linked to the command in Sid, but it is not the command in Sid but the KOG, the counter-intelligence group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I apologise for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we are interrupting, page 13, on our screen, line 14, it indicates that the chief of security of the 80th Brigade was Colonel Sljivancanin. Is that the answer that was given? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me? No. No, of course not. I was the chief of security of the 80th Brigade, and the colonel was the chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade and also the chief of security of the OG South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, does this mean that during this period of time, which was obviously shorter, when you were subordinated to the Guards Brigade and its security organ, does it mean that you did not issue any written reports at all, or that you didn't do it as often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you -- you made a slip of a tongue. Between the subordinate and the superior. Let me ask you a question. I wrote one or two reports for Captain Karan, and everything else was in verbal form. But there was not much cooperation because the 80th Brigade did not have a lot of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the hierarchal structure had to be respected; you couldn't skip a level. I'm talking about the security organs line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not unless that was requested, because, as a rule, everything went along the normal lines in the security matters; it was just one of the regular services in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about your attitude to your own commander, or position to your own commander, you were his formal assistant for security, as the chief of the security organ, and you said - I am going to quote - that the most important security-related information of the unit was something that the brigade commander was informed about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the security matters in the unit were told to the commander, according to the security line. Nothing was concealed from him. Anything he needed in order to execute his command duties, he would receive from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All that related to the security of the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that relate to information of a counter-intelligence nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Everything or only what was approved by your superior along the security organ line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the time that a commander receives information is crucial. If something is late, then that information is no longer of any use, either to you or to him. So in that sense the security organ has the ability to assess this and to pass on the information. So I would always, without fail, inform the commander, and then after that I would inform the security organs in the superior command. Even together with my security officers in the battalions I would inform the battalion commanders about certain problems so that they would be able to have all this information at their disposal while they were making their command decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that the tasks that you performed as a security organ, as part of those tasks, some are directly related to work in the brigade as opposed to the intelligence or counter-intelligence type of activities, and that that work in the brigade itself is first of all military police, administrative and criminal activities, and that they directly relate to the brigade commander along this line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot agree with you entirely. We can agree on the part which is defined by the rules of service for the work of the security organs. So my function would be a control function. In relation to the police, I controlled their work, their training, I possibly suggest their use. As far as criminal proceedings are concerned, the brigade commander has the assistant for morale, who is at the same time assistant for legal affairs. So legal affairs and anything that is criminal related would be in the jurisdiction of the organ for morale and not the organ for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So then you take that some of the duties were not in your remit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. Legal matters are in the domain of the assistant for morale, political and legal matters. So he would be the one to initiate proceedings in terms of what perhaps the public prosecutor does. And if a military tribunal is formed at the level of the brigade, then this assistant can also serve as the presiding judge of that tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this specific situation, was it possible to form a military tribunal? Did something like that -- was something like that possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the brigade didn't have anything like that. Nobody actually insisted that we deal with legal matters. No security organ in the JNA would deal with legal matters. This would be something that the morale organ would be in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, the bulk of your duties were counter-intelligence and of an intelligence nature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we can agree, just as Mr. Moore asked me here yesterday, my assignments were primarily of a counter-intelligence nature. As part of the duties of the Chief of Staff, there is an operations organ and an organ for intelligence matters, and that organ deals with intelligence issues. I am under the commander, but the chief for intelligence is linked to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you perhaps assess or tell us what the percentages were of your engagement in this sense?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I answered your question already: I was 100 per cent engaged on counter-intelligence duties, just as the 100 per cent engagement of the chief for intelligence would be to work on intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vojnovic [as interpreted], when we're talking about informing the commander about all that pertains to the security of the unit assessments data and so on, there is a term, and you will correct me if I am wrong, but it says in the required -- to the acquired [as interpreted] extent, and level. Could you please tell me what that means.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said Mr. Vojnovic. Did you mean Mr. Vukosavljevic, myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, did you convey to Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am obliged, as the security chief, to give all the information to the brigade commander - in this case Vojnovic - that are essential for the purposes of executing command and control functions of the brigade. There is no holding back. It's all absolute. If you're late with an information, then that is useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But, Mr. Vukosavljevic, if it says "to the required extent and degree," does that mean you are the one who assesses this required level and degree, or is there somebody else who would make that assessment in passing on information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you found that, "to the required extent and degree." That would imply absolutely the extent to which the commander can have available information at his disposal so that he can make decisions which affect the security of the unit. That is that measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please tell me something about the area of responsibility of your 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the 80th Motorised Brigade had an area of responsibility. When I came on the 8th, I asked the commander to inform me about the situation. At that point in time, he didn't have any orders relating to the use of units, meaning he didn't have any orders so that the area of responsibility of the 80th Brigade could not have been formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If not then, how about later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 23rd and 24th we did receive orders from the 1st Military District command. The war assignment was formed for the 80th Brigade battalions, and artillery battalions received their assignments and the brigade was assigned its area of responsibility, and it began to draft documents, combat documents, regulating, amongst other things, the area of responsibility. On the working map at brigade command, the brigade's area of responsibility and the deployment of its subordinate units is marked precisely on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: For example, Ovcara, Grabovo, Jakubovac; such places?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were in the area of responsibility. Well, to tell you the truth, at the brigade level, we only had one working map. According to the rules of service, the brigade organ for security should have a working map too. I should have done that. However, I did not have to carry out that duty. The commander told me I didn't need to do that. The command didn't have two working maps, it only had one working map that was for the whole OG. Even the commander didn't have his own working map that he was duty-bound to maintain. So I really cannot be very specific in my answer about the 80th Brigade's area of responsibility after the 23rd, 24th and 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before the 23rd, 4th and 5th, I'm asking you, and I think you said before - I will remind you - you also mentioned in your statements the local commanders, one of these places that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this was something that was decided on by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, so were these places in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you specifically, but we need to go into semi-private --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're going to continue with the same topic, the security organ of which you were chief, and you had started to talk about this. After the departure of the Guards Motorised Brigade, you talked about several dates; 23rd, 22nd, 24th. I don't know if we can agree that your brigade entered Vukovar on the 22nd of November, and there is an order of the 22nd that you were talking about. We are going to establish that on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be best to establish that on the basis of documents because I don't have all the dates in my head. It's been over 14 years since then, so please don't take it ill, but I cannot remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In any case, this was at the time when the Guards Brigade was leaving Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Guards Brigade left Vukovar on the 24th of November in the morning, or perhaps you don't even remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is -- well, I don't know that there were any Guards Brigade units in Vukovar on the 23rd. I think most of those units were in the village of Negoslavci. This is what I know. But I'm not asserting that, I'm just answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. From that period, a day or two before or after, as you say, your superiors along the security organs line were in Sid. Your immediate contact was with the counter-intelligence group in Sid, headed by Colonel Ljubisa Perkovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction: It's Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic, not Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it as Petkovic, and that's how I responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But it's just a mistake in the transcript, and of course it's important that we have the correct transcript. Could you please tell me who Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Professionally.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the -- a colonel in the Sid command [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know him professionally before that or did you get to know him when you began to directly cooperate with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got to know him when we started to work together. It was the first time that I actually saw him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I do have another intervention. You said colonel in Sid, but in the transcript on page 22, line 21, it says the Sid command. So this is another correction. It's the COG, counter-intelligence group in Sid?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what a KOG is, a counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a general answer: It's a group made up of officers who are involved in counter-intelligence work, using the methods and means used in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that group of officers would have its network of associates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I really wouldn't like to answer that because I don't believe that I have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Vukosavljevic, that we do have the right to find out about this, that that cannot be a secret matter that you were -- did not receive a waiver for.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it here in the document that I can talk about the methods of operation or work of the counter-intelligence service. I don't have a decision of the government saying that I can talk about the methods of work of the counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But do you have explicitly it stated that you cannot talk about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not stressed that I can, so I assume that I cannot, based on the confidentiality oath that I stated and because of the rules of my service. You know that if it's not explicitly stated, it's something that I cannot talk about. You are a lawyer, you should know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think now we have come again to the point where I quite rightly asked you to read the document, even though it's a decision. Could you please read the part of it that says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet. The first time that this officer says that he came under the area of responsibility of the counter-intelligence group in Sid was, as I understand it, about the 23rd of November. How is it going to assist the determination of this case to learn whether that group had or did not have a team of officers working on counter-intelligence work? Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this line of questioning can be explained by the fact that this counter-intelligence group existed, it was led by Colonel Petkovic, the witness did not have any contacts with it prior to a certain period of time, and my question is to find out how this counter-intelligence group worked at the time, especially in view of my following question about Captain Karanfilov that you spoke about, and I was going to ask you whether he was a member of that counter-intelligence group in Sid. That was going to be my next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We know from evidence that a Captain Karanfilov was in the area of Ovcara, dealing with prisoners from Mitnica at various times, at least on the 18th and 19th of November. Are you able to say from which unit Captain Karanfilov came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, he came from the Guards Motorised Brigade. As far as I know, I'm saying. But Mr. Domazet's question is different, and I believe that he was absolutely from the Guards Motorised Brigade, not from the counter-intelligence group Sid, as purported by Mr. Domazet. This is what I know. If there are any documents speaking differently, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Domazet is interested in your knowledge. And perhaps that meets your need, does it, Mr. Domazet? As far as this witness is concerned, he was not from the Sid counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few more questions about that, and I will bring this topic to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were talking about your reports and sending them regularly and that you had personal contacts, that you attended meetings; this is what you spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where was the seat of the counter-intelligence group in Sid where you attended meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After such a long time, I can't tell you. This is a secret [as interpreted], but in any case, it is in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is where the meetings took place that you attended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings took place at different places, not at the post office where the seat of the counter-intelligence group was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You answered, but it says in the transcript that this is a secret. However, you said it was not a secret, that was in the post office in Sid.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bear in mind that time and -- I believe that this is not a secret, and yes, it was in the post office in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your answer is good, but it did not enter the transcript correctly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a secret of a sort, but it is not such a big secret, and especially given the time that has lapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it also true that -- you said that the officers were members of the counter-intelligence group. Are you saying that all the officers were members of the counter-intelligence group, or only a few of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every counter-intelligence group is composed of the counter-intelligence officers who are members of that group. And then they receive from their superior tasks to cover a certain unit, and so on and so forth. But a counter-intelligence group as such is an autonomous group, it is autonomous in its activities, and it is subordinated to one of the commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do they have a direct command link with which security organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just been asked to come closer to the microphone. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you repeat your last answer, because there has been another error in the transcript. It is about the counter-intelligence group which is independent, autonomous, and that its activities are under the command of a superior command. You didn't say that, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did. Mr. Domazet, let us clarify your previous question. You asked me about the way of reporting, and the meetings with the officers from the Sid group. I said that these meetings were in Sid, but also elsewhere on the ground. I wanted to provide that precise answer to your question. And now when we're talking about the security line, the chain goes to the chief of the security administration, and every group that is subordinated to anybody starts with independent battalions where there are security organs, then in brigades, and it is all linked to a superior command. In other words, there is no autonomy as such; there is a vertical hierarchy which ends up with the top of the pyramid, that is how it's organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but you are talking about the command along the line of security.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the profession is the line in question. But the commanders of the units are also the commanders of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now let's go back to the counter-intelligence group in Sid. According to you, whether the security administration was its superior organ.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that the security organ never asks its superior security organ who they're linked to. It is their secret and it is up to them to reveal the secret or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you saying that you yourself didn't know that, or you do not want to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I did not say it is not a secret; I really did not know to Mr. Ljubisa Petkovic was subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When it comes to prisoners of war, do they fall under the purview of counter-intelligence that the security organ is in charge of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to prisoners of war, there are several services that should get involved, and every service has to do its segment of the job. The first contact that prisoners of war have anyone is with the intelligence service who are to find out who they are and where they come from, how strong their forces are. And then one segment of the work can be carried out by the assistant for morale and guidance who is also in charge of certain jobs to do with psychology, and they have to separate those who were -- who committed crimes against the civilian population, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this done by the security organ in your brigade, in the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have many prisoners of war. We only had this Mitnica group. We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I continue while the counsel confers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had this Mitnica group that we guarded just one night. They were our charge for just one night. And the hospital group was there for three or four hours, and I was there only for half an hour, not longer. And in practical terms we did not have any other prisoners of war. I believe that there was a group in the barracks, and as soon as the brigade arrived, they were transported to Sid. So what I'm saying is that we did not have an opportunity to get involved in that field of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well, then, we will come to that. But before that, let's try and correct a mistake in the transcript on page 28, lines 3 and 4. When you were talking about certain things, and it says here that those who were in charge of morale guidance were also in charge of prisoners of war, but you were talking about that separately, as a separate thing from the security organ that gets involved with the prisoners of war. Did you go, together with Captain Vezmarovic, to look for a suitable location for the accommodation of prisoners and that's how you arrived in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me correct you. Captain Vezmarovic is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you are clear who I'm talking about. So can you tell us -- can you give me the answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go, I did not choose the location, but what is the specific situation that you are referring when you're talking about this and when you're asking me whether I went to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'll tell you because Captain Vezmarovic testified before this Chamber and he said that he went with you and that he first went to Ovcara and that the two of you chose that location as a camp for prisoners, that you started with Ovcara, that you stayed there, and that you chose that location as the prisoner camp.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't go with Captain Vezmarovic to choose a location for the prisoners of war. As far as I can remember, this is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, could my learned friend direct me to the part of the transcript where Vezmarovic says that? Because I'm trying to find it as best I can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise, it is not Captain Vezmarovic. The information that I have is that the witness went to -- with Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So my question now is whether you ever went with Colonel Vojnovic to look for such a location.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. But who provided you with that information? If you are asking me that question, I would like to know where that information comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question is whether you were -- went with Colonel Vojnovic, but you say you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First you said Vezmarovic, now you say Vojnovic. This is bordering on speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the security administration sent high-ranking security officers to control that part of your work, the work with the prisoners of war at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Given your position, should you be in the position to know that? And if anybody had come, would they have to come to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only polite for those who arrive in somebody's territory to contact their hosts. In other words, whenever Mr. Petkovic arrived, he would announce his visit, he would come and say hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the role of the security organ in the selection of people, and I believe you were referring to the interrogation of those prisoners of war, I would like to ask you whether you know where this was done with the prisoners of war from this territory.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I put it to you that this was done in Sremska Mitrovica, would you still maintain the same position and would you say that you never participated in that personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are putting it to me that it was in Sremska Mitrovica, I can tell you that you are right. In Sremska Mitrovica there was a detention unit where prisoners of war were sent, and to the -- to a question by Mr. Moore, I did say that they were sent there. And as far as I know, there were a number of counter-intelligence officers working there, collecting information from the prisoners of war who were in the detention unit in Sremska Mitrovica, so you are right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know anything, as a security officer at the time, that anything was being said and that there were different orders about exchanges of prisoners, exchanges with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, for example, that Dr. Bosanac was exchanged, and I believe that two other members of the Croatian ethnicity were exchanged together with her on the same night. And I also saw on TV that a whole group from Sremska Mitrovica was either released or exchanged. I saw Mr. Filip Karaula on TV - he had been in Mitnica on that night - and I saw on TV that he was one of those who was involved in that exchange. But that was six or seven months before, or a year -- later, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But this -- this was later, everybody is familiar with that, this was done publicly. But I am talking about the relevant period of time. Were there some orders issued that arrived at your address, talking about exchanges, exchanges being arranged, organised, banned, or so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such orders, and as a matter of principle, this is humanitarian work and all the sides are involved in it. This is a positive thing in any war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday my learned friend asked you about evacuations in Vukovar and you spoke about the first evacuation as the evacuation of people from Borovo Naselje that went through Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, however, that there was another evacuation exercise involving civilians, women, children and elderly that went in the direction of Vinkovci and, as far as we know, it was returned midway?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that event. I know that on our TV, while I was still not mobilised, there was a report on the evacuation of the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital, but I don't know any details but those that were shown on TV. As a security organ, I was never involved in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question doesn't relate only to your operative work. Did you hear about this matter from Borovo Naselje operationally, or did you just -- or were you involved with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just heard about it. Later I found out exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Regarding the evacuation of prisoners, let's call it that, the evacuation from Mitnica, you know what it is all about; you spoke about that in detail yesterday. And according to what you said, there were no particular problems there, either in the security, departure, or detention of those persons, except for the case of a drunken lieutenant-colonel who had come and also some individuals who came and tried to get to those people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In that case, the prisoners were there in the afternoon, the whole night, and then until the next morning, and you and Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic and a captain of the military police throughout that whole time except for the time when you maybe sometimes went away, you were there, and then immediately before they left, you left to rest, and this was granted by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right when you said that there was some occasional times when we left. There was none of that. We were there the whole time, and it wasn't according to the order of Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, but the order of Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Danilovic was leading the operation, but the -- but immediately before the prisoners were boarded, Vojnovic came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I think that you said that Vojnovic had sent you to rest before those people left, and Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic was with you the day before, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard you say Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, and not Vojnovic, and that's why I am correcting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, it's in the transcript, so that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I would like to move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you explained that there were no problems with the Mitnica group, so why was not the same procedure used with this last group, then, the group from the Vukovar Hospital? And you know which group I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what group we're talking about, but I have to tell you that it's strange to me why the same procedure was not applied in that case, because simply according to what I know, and according to what the brigade commander told me about that, he and the brigade did not receive any orders. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we're talking now -- we're going to move now to a discrete topic and we're only five minutes away from our regular break, I think that perhaps this would be a convenient time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukosavljevic, we began on the topic of evacuations. You said that you remembered the evacuations, you talked about them, you said that you remembered the evacuation of prisoners from Mitnica. The next group that we talked about was the group from the hospital. My question is whether, in the interval between those two evacuations the departure of the group from Mitnica and the arrival of this other group, did any other group come and was it guarded in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Specifically, a group -- the group of the Mitnica detainees was taken to Sremska Mitrovica in the morning of the 19th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 19th in the evening a large group that had been turned back from the highway, a group in several buses, spent the night at Ovcara and was guarded by the 80th Motorised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know where you get that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These were civilians. As the intelligence organ or security organ, did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't any anything about that. I don't know where that information comes from. I would probably have known about it, if it had happened. It's probably another mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, it's not. Let me just refresh your memory. Perhaps you will recall that representatives of international organisations were present at the time and that night the International Red Cross came and the group left on the 20th in the morning. You, as the security organ, I assume would have to know that, even though -- if you didn't participate in that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must have known -- I ought to know about it even though that I do not know. So I must have done my job badly, if I don't know about it. However, I doubt that I did my job badly, because I don't remember that group. It's not likely that it was there. But as I say, if I don't know about that group, I must have done my job badly, but I don't think that I did my job badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And now we're going to talk about this last group that you know about very well. I think that earlier when I asked you how was it that the group was not secured in the same way as the group from Mitnica, you said that it was not announced, and that this presented -- I think what you wanted to say was -- was some sort of a surprise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered your question by saying that it was not clear to me why it wasn't done like that 100 per cent, but there is a transcript, so we would perhaps need to read that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to try and lift your voice louder. At times you speak very clearly, but at other times your voice becomes very soft. And when it becomes very soft, the microphones are not able to pick it up well enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honour, to -- to be heard better. Is it -- am I already louder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are a little louder, but you are still very soft.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will try to raise my voice, but I don't want you to think that I am nervous and that I am shouting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you want to shout, go right ahead. We've heard plenty of that in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We will go on, Mr. Vukosavljevic. My question about this group is the following: You, as the security organ, were you informed about the arrival of that group in advance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody told me anything about the arrival of that group. The first information about it was, like I told the Prosecutor, when the commander told me to go and see what was going on there. So only when I arrived I found out that it was a group of prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this was when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the late afternoon, or actually at dusk on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So my question whether this was something that you knew about it on the 19th, before the afternoon or dusk, as you say.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is an entry about it in the war diary of the 80th Motorised Brigade on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. A war diary is not something that a security organ would be interested in. This is something that is recorded by the Chief of Staff and the duty officer in the staff. I didn't follow what was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Even though you didn't read it, if something like that was in the war diary, that would clearly indicate that that was something that was known about at the time it was recorded in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was known to the person who made the entry and the person who instructed the entry to be made. I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 375 now. Could it be put on the monitor. And it's an entry for the 19th of November at 1800 hours. And I would like to apologise, we tried to provide hard copies, but the copier is not working, so we only have some copies available. But I hope that this will not be that long, and that we will be able to ... We also have the English translation, and it's for the 19th, at 1800 hours. And it says the following: "Surrender of the remaining ZNG and MUP members is expected (about 200), and it's necessary to be prepared to guard these prisoners." Do you stand by what you said, that you were not informed about it and that you didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I said, that I didn't know about this information. But reading this, this is really a general piece of information, and it refers to the Vukovar Hospital in general. If you agree, surrender of ZNG, and so on, is expected. The Vukovar Hospital is not mentioned. So this is practically in the sphere of an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please look more closely. "In the region of the hospital," it says. It's in line 4 in B/C/S: "Combat is going on in the area of the hospital where the surrender of the ZNG is being expected."

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right, sir. I didn't read it correctly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this is consistent with what happened the following day, both in terms of numbers and the substance as stated herein.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I didn't know about the existence of this diary and this particular entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me how it is possible that you, as the security organ, are not informed, either through the chain of command or through the professional security line, you were not, in fact, aware of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't along any of these lines that I was informed about this particular piece of information, nor did I know about the contents of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well, let us move on to the 20th of November in the afternoon, and this particular point in time is very important, and please focus. Tell us when it was exactly that you learned about this and went over to Ovcara. You said that it was at dusk, however we know that in the month of November days draw in, and can you tell us when it was exactly that you arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered the question put by the Prosecutor. I said that I arrived there at about 1700 or 1730 hours. Now, if you're interested about who I arrived with, I've already stated that, but I can go through that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will try to avoid repetition as far as possible. You said that you arrived with two officers there. My question is, did you -- were you ordered to do that, or did you yourself choose the officers that would go with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the brigade commander who told me, and assigned these two officers to go with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this a verbal order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a verbal order, and these officers were answerable to the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will tell me if I'm mistaken, to speed up the process, you thought that it was at about 1700, 1730 hours because this was the time of the dusk?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although this was quite a long time ago, and I cannot state this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You stayed there for about 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then you headed in the vehicle back, leaving the two officers behind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir. I have to -- do I have to correct something in my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, no. Just please wait for my question to be put to you in its entirety. Observe the transcript so that we do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also told us about the time necessary for the trip. You even stated yesterday that during this trip in this car with the driver, that you regretted the fact that you left the two officers behind and were heading back alone, or just the two of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, this trip did not take that long, so when was it, approximately, that you reached your command and went to see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it could have taken some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move through this quickly. You didn't find him, you were told that he was in the command with Colonel Mrksic, attending a meeting or a briefing that they had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That he was in a meeting where they were briefed, something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that a briefing was held with Colonel Mrksic every day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that it was held there every day, but I do know that the commander went to the Guards Motorised Brigade for briefing. Whether this was a daily occurrence or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that these briefings were held before 1800 hours because, among other things, at 1800 hours a report was compiled to be sent to the commander of the military district, does this accord with your memory of these events, or are you not aware of this at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this at all, but I'm sure that Colonel Vojnovic, brigade commander, was familiar with this and I suppose you could deal with this with him. As far as briefings are concerned, yes, I do agree that they might have been held at a particular hour every day, but I was not privy to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on your statement, you arrived there and waited quite a long time for the meeting to end. First you stated that you waited for about two hours, then you corrected your statement and said that it lasted for about an hour and a half. But even this period of time is quite long. You had ample time to observe the premises where you were waiting quite well. Can you describe for us where it was that you stood or where you were sitting, who was present in the room with you, what the rooms were like and where were they.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the house where the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade was. It was the largest house in Negoslavci. On the right-hand side, as one enters the house, there was a staircase, and it was like a hallway, because there wasn't much furniture there. And there was a warrant officer there and two or three police officers who stood in front of the door to the room where the meeting was held. The driver who brought me there had orders to return back to his post as soon as possible, and as I was waiting there for quite a long time, he came to ask me what he was to do. I expected the meeting to end quite soon, based on what the warrant officer there told me, because normally the commander, when discussing matters with the security officer, this is something that he would do with his closest associates eye to eye. That was why I had to wait outside, and I was walking to and fro, waiting for the meeting to end. However, by the time I realised that the meeting was not going to end that soon, I told the driver to go back to his post and that we would see what we would do. Then Rajacic, a commander of a police battalion, arrived. He was in my brigade in November to conduct an inspection. He took me to a dining hall there, and he asked me whether I wanted to have something to eat. And of course I accepted gladly because I didn't have a chance to eat regularly. We talked there, he told me that he had arrived from Sid with an armoured combat vehicle in order to take on some Croatian soldiers for some exchange. I spent about an hour with Rajacic in this dining-room of the command of the Guards Brigade. When the meeting ended, I saw the officers coming out of the room, I went upstairs, and met Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and I told him what I had already stated in my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The dining-room is something that you mention now for the first time. Is that in the same building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same building but in the basement. So one had to go down the stairs to the basement. So it wasn't the ground level, but the basement level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You tell us now that you were there until the meeting ended and officers started coming out of the meeting room.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember who these officers were. Did you know any of them, and how many of them did go out of the room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a few officers. I didn't know them, I can't tell you their names, but there were quite a few of them. Your colleague, I believe his name is Vasic, if I remember well, he asked whether this was just a meeting between Mr. General [as interpreted] and Colonel Mrksic. The gentleman is right that this was a meeting involving large numbers of officers from the staff. Mr. Vojnovic was the subordinated commander, so in addition to staff members, there were subordinated commanders, in addition to the members of the staff of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand. Please try and be more specific. This group of officers, how many of them were there, in fact? Can you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, you would say that a group consists of three to five soldiers. In these terms I would say that this was larger than a group. There were more of them than just a group, but I cannot be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Therefore, you did not recognise anyone save your commander, Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us the ranks of these officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of them were officers holding ranks from captain above. Well, I can't say that they -- all the ranks were represented, but they were senior officers. That's an observation on my part. I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. And you tell us that it was then that you saw your commander, Vojnovic, you approached him and told him then what you already stated.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you told him how concerned you were about the Ovcara situation. Yesterday, in response to my learned friend's questions, you stated that somewhat later you talked with Colonel Mrksic personally and that was in the room where the meeting was held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were examined on this particular matter on several occasions. Let's recall the first such examination, which was in Novi Sad before an investigating magistrate, and you also gave a statement to investigators involved in the Ovcara trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
