utterances.text: Two to three days after the Sablja operation, I gave a statement to the investigators of the Serbian police. I also gave a statement at the trial against Sasa Radak, who I had never seen in my life before, I want to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the statements we have before us, the statements that are available to us. If you recall, when you were giving a statement to investigators, you were presented with this Novi Sad statement, and at the very beginning you furnished very accurate corrections to that statement. There were two or three, four or five things that you wanted to rectify.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can enumerate them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mrksic, not Brksic; it was Vezmarovic, not Bezmarovic; and then there was some time I had to rectify; and I cannot recall the fourth point. You would have to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, let me see.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you think it's important, then please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, something concerning the immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right, sir. My immediate commander was Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's correct. But I will draw your attention to a portion of this statement which does not [Realtime transcript read in error "in the"] accord with what you stated here yesterday, and you did not ask to rectify this particular part. Although you stated that you remembered that there were some misspellings of names, perhaps this is something that you do remember, and it has to do with your encounter and conversation with Colonel Mrksic, which we just mentioned a moment ago. I'm faced with a difficulty, which is -- well, I would kindly ask that the English version be placed on the monitor, which is ET 0299-2626. This is page 3, where I'd like to read out a couple of lines. If you have the Serbian version, you can follow, or if not, you can listen to me reading, but perhaps I should ask the usher's assistance in handing the witness the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, Mr. Domazet, page 46 on our screen, line 17, I think the answer was -- or your question was which does not accord with what you stated. The transcript suggests you said it was in accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, it must be an error. I can't find it now. But at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's in your favour, Mr. Domazet. Don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is the first statement, practically page 1, toward the end of page 1. Perhaps some 10 lines from the bottom, where you said that you briefed Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic on the situation and then it says: "And then Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic went with me to Colonel Mrksic and introduced me to him as brigade commander. I informed him of the problem. I furnished the details. Colonel Mrksic said that he had other obligations to attend to, and that he didn't have the time to deal with this matter, and to put it colloquially, he simply brushed him off." And then the following line: "There upon Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic reviewed or considered the situation --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have no problems at all about the question, but if it's going to be put to the witness, surely what was said must be accurately repeated by my learned friend. With regard to the English translation, there were two reasons given, and my learned friend has only given one. Perhaps it would be easier just to read it. I see my learned friend's concern, but that's certainly my understanding from the document I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the Chamber is at a disadvantage. We are told the document has not been provided in English and so is not available electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am assuming that my learned friend is referring from the OTP witness statement. He did say at the beginning, but in actual fact it's page 12 of the OTP statement. I'm working on the basis that that's what the cross-examination is on, in relation to that statement and no other. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smith [as interpreted] is right. You were looking at the OTP statement, and I'm reading from the Novi Sad statement, and hence the discrepancy. I am reading the Serbian version, the B/C/S version of the Novi Sad statement. We have two copies for the Trial Chamber. If we could ask the usher to provide the Trial Chamber with the copies. We don't have any more copies, unfortunately, because the photocopier was out of order. And hence the mistake -- I am pointing to this fact because, as Mr. Moore has said, there is a significant discrepancy between the OTP statement and the Novi Sad statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, I am reading the statement that you gave in Novi Sad, Mr. Vukosavljevic. I'm going to read the relevant part again, I'm going to read it carefully, and this is the translation that does exist. This has been translated into English. We have provided it to the Trial Chamber. This is on page 3 towards the end of that page, and at the beginning of page 4, the first paragraph on that page. I'll start as follows: "Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic --" I apologise. I'm reading the relevant sentences. After the meeting with Vojnovic, you told him what was happening. And then the next sentence that I deem important reads: "Thereupon Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic went together to see Mrksic and introduced me as the commander of the brigade --" this is erroneous, but that doesn't matter. "... informed him about the problem and I filled him in with the details of the situation. Colonel Mrksic said that he had other obligations, and that he didn't have the time to resolve that and, to put it colloquially, he just brushed me off." And then the next passage which reads -- In the transcript we have, "... he brushed me off," although in the original it says "he brushed him off"; i.e., this brushing off does not refer to Vojnovic. "After that, Lieutenant-Colonel considered the situation and told me that I had convey to Captain Vezmarovic the message to withdraw the military unit from the security of Ovcara, and he never explained to me how and to whom Captain Vezmarovic was supposed to hand over the prisoners." Is this what reads in the passage, with all the mistakes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there are mistakes here. The whole transcript is rather full of mistakes. It says here, "Thereupon Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic went together to see Mrksic," it should have stated together with me. There are a lot of mistakes. And then he introduced me as the brigade commander. I was not the brigade commander. This is another mistake on the part of the Prosecution and my mistake. As far as the entire statement is concerned - and this was taken by the Prosecutor in Novi Sad - it is rather archaic. I have corrected three or four mistakes, and for that reason I did ask to be given an opportunity to authorise my statement given to The Hague Tribunal, and if you have that document, you will see that I signed every page of that second document in order to avoid the repetition of such mistakes. As far as the whole procedure is concerned, as I have already told before this Trial Chamber and before the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, I would like to adhere to this: I would like to remind you of another thing that you know as a lawyer, and it has to do with the way you're being interviewed. Mr. Mijovic [phoen] was in haste, I was the last witness on his list for interview and he did not ask me the same questions you are putting to me now. He did not go into any details as it is being done here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I can partially agree with what you are saying. I am pointing to some of the mistakes, but the ones that I do not consider important -- the fact that you were introduced as the brigade commander, that is not important; the fact that you were not mentioned as a person who went with him to see Mrksic, it is clear from the context. But the statement was dictated to you and you signed every page, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It probably flows from the witness, but the English translation that I have is that -- clearly shows that they did travel, or he did travel with Vojnovic. Phrases like, "Thereupon Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic went together ... and introduced me ..." Now, that's on the English translation. It can't be said that he's just been taken individually. I know the witness did say that, but it's clearly not correct from the translation. There is a reference to Vojnovic going together and "introduced me." So that has to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the English translation of the original Serbian statement, and I read it out in the Serbian, and it says here: "Colonel Vojnovic together went to Mrksic."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that what it says in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In other words, they went together. Maybe this has been translated erroneously in the English version, but this is the original. Yesterday you told us that Mrksic left the room, then you approached him. It says here that together with Vojnovic you went to see him, and that is a big difference which has nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Domazet. I didn't understand any evidence of the witness yesterday to say that Mrksic left the room before there was a conversation between Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, this witness, and Colonel Mrksic. He said there was that conversation in the room, and then Colonel Mrksic went to leave through a doorway at the far end of the room, and Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic escorted him at least part of the way to the doorway. And then this Vojnovic returned and this witness and Vojnovic spoke after the colonel had left. Now, that is my recollection of the evidence of this witness. You were putting something, I think, quite different at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness is best suited to say what happened, whether he spoke in the office or in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hallway. And if that had been put to me as a question in Novi Sad, I would have said that. The whole statement, the record of what I said, is rather archaic, I have just said that. Full of mistakes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, would you agree with me there is a difference in the fact whether the conversation took place in the hallway or in the office, as is stated here, and I will accept your answer, but is it true what it says here, that Colonel Mrksic, to the two of you, said, which you never disputed or corrected in the subsequent intervention, that he said to you that he had other obligations and that he didn't have the time to resolve this matter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to the general for the jargon, and when you give an interview sometimes you can't find the right word, and I apologise for using this, General, but he did brush me off. I did use this jargon word, I apologise. I didn't find a better term at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is no need for you to apologise, this is what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think that there is a need for me to apologise and that's why I'm doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But it says here that Vojnovic personally considered the situation afterwards and then that he told you what you should convey to Captain Vezmarovic. Yesterday, however, you said that after that there was a conversation that you partially heard, partially did not hear, you don't know what they were saying, and you never mentioned that subsequent conversation, the conversation that you did not listen to. Do you agree that there is no mention in the Novi Sad statement about that conversation, about that subsequent conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I believe that there is an approach in the interview that was taken in Novi Sad, the approach of the interviewer there and the interviewers here in The Hague. The questions that were put to me there differed from the questions that are put to me here now. I don't see any problem here. I do not see any contradiction here with what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we then agree that what you stated here is correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here in this statement. No. I believe that this record is very bad, that the sentences are incomplete, there is no logic to some of them, and I believe this cannot be used to seek difference -- differences which are practically not there, in my view. I did sign this record, I am not disputing that. I was the last witness on that day, everybody was in a hurry, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But let's go back to this. It says here that after you were brushed off by Colonel Mrksic, Colonel Vojnovic considered the situation. After his consideration, he told you what to do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are sticking to this phrase "consideration." I can't tell you anything in that sense. This is what it says in the record. After we -- our consultations with Mr. Mrksic, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic ordered me to convey the order to Captain Vezmarovic to withdraw the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He didn't tell you then what to do with the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And let's be very precise - and you are also under the oath here - you didn't hear Colonel Mrksic saying anything to that effect on that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear him issue an order to colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic on the withdrawal of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you mention before Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic that it might be in order to issue a written instruction, or you never discussed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity as a security organ, I was not in charge of command. I did not command over any unit, and I did not need such an order from him. Whether he was supposed to ask for a written order from his superior commander, that was up to him. It was his choice. I couldn't do anything about that. It was not my call. We might have discussed it, but I don't remember having discussed that with Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will agree that you thought that your role was to convey the message?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a courier, although this was not within my purview, but that's what I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because of the fact that you did not have the right to issue any such order, and according to your own words, you acted as a courier, was it then necessary to have a written order of the Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying this. The rule of service -- the rules of service for the work of the security organs says that. It says that the security organ does not command any units in the military police. My view in that respect is not important. This is what is regulated by the rules of service, and there is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In legal terms you do have a certain influence on the military police, but this is beyond our topic now. I'm talking about the order by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. Since you didn't have the right to issue any orders, you only could act as a courier, and in light of that fact, was it necessary for him to issue any orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been the commander of the military police company who could have asked him to do that. It was not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well then. But as far as I understand you, you are still not sure whether you ever conveyed that message to Captain Vezmarovic, given the situation that you found on the spot; you could see them already getting ready to -- for movement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you now go back to the timing that we started discussing already. I believe that after the conversation with Vojnovic you went back to Ovcara. How long did it take you to get there, and can you remember, when was it that you arrived in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can do the math together, sir, but let me tell you, after 14 and a half years, it's very difficult for me to remember exactly how long it took. In my first interview in 2003, this was 12 years after the event, which is still a long time, and I can't tell you exactly how long it took. We can just arrive at some conclusions as to how long it took. We can do the math together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You can, or we can try.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could do it together. This is how I see it. If I was there at around 1730 hours, then arrived at the command at 18, 1810 hours, then waited for an hour and a half, that's 1930 hours. Then I came back at about 2000 hours, or between 20 and 2100 hours. That would be an approximate time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If it was 1730 hours, and you will allow that it gets dark even before that, perhaps it was even earlier than that. If we take that briefing as some kind of pointer, it was supposed to have finished at 1800 hours, the briefing with Mrksic, and then the report was submitted from that meeting -- was supposed to be submitted at 1800 hours, would that change the time, that the meeting ended at 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, sir, it's very hard to ask me to talk about precise times after 14 years. I didn't know when the briefing was at the headquarters of OG South or the 80th Motorised Brigade. I don't know if the meeting was long or short, but I know that the part that I attended was one and a half hours. I was there at 1800 hours, and I think I -- it went on until about 1930 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But we can take it that immediately after the conversation with Vojnovic and what he told you, you went back and you reached Ovcara quite quickly. And I think something else, and you said that you abide by that, that practically you didn't say there for a long time, that you picked up, in a way, some of these two officers, put them in your vehicle, and you brought them back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you are aware that there is a note in the operations log-book that at 2235 hours the pull-out took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that entry, and when I was replying to your questions, that's what I had in mind. However, as you said, I personally -- I have to stick to the truth. I personally believe that the duty officer who was -- who made the entry might have extended the time a little bit. I think the unit came back earlier. I think -- I'm not saying anything; an official document is an official document, and as far as I'm concerned, as a security organ, it's an official document. But I think that perhaps the duty officer extended the time a bit. I know this information, I talked about this on the basis of my recollection. So I stand by what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not fix the time, although I know that in the war diary it states 2235, but I am giving my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that in response to a question by my learned friend you said that you conveyed to Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic on the way back that you replied that everything was in the spirit of the order that he gave. Did I understand you correctly, what you said yesterday, did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So literally you did not tell him that you had conveyed the order and ordered in his name, ordered Captain Vezmarovic to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just commented on that. We felt that the job was done in the spirit of the order, and that is how we acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about the way it was done, don't you think that as the intelligence, or rather, the security organ, you were obliged in respect of the prisoners of war to see or to express an interest in what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, everything is of interest to the security organ. But, in this case, no particular reserve, in terms of what would happen, did I express, because from what I understood, my commander received an order from his superior commander. And I, as the security organ, was not in touch with the volunteers and TO units and so on and so forth. My commander also was not in contact. We practically, as far as I understood, he received an order from the commander of the southern front, which was in joint coordinated action with the members of those units that were at Ovcara. And as far as I know, this coordinated action went on for longer than a month or a month and a half. So he is in a position to know much better than I am, or my commander. Secondly, the units that remained were, according to what I know, under the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Practically, I did not permit myself to teach or instruct someone who, in the military sense, is better educated or trained than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this quite lengthy answer it states - and it is in English - I would like you to clarify this order from the commander of the OG South. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated in English. You were listening to me in Serbian and we understand each other very well, that I assumed that my commander received an order from his superior commander, from the commander of OG South, to pull out. So that commander, in -- as part of his forces, had units that remained at Ovcara. So anyone who hangs a rifle on their shoulder must be familiar with The Hague conventions. So whoever was in charge or had anything to do with guarding the prisoners had to have been informed or had to have known about The Hague conventions. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course I have to agree with you. I agree with what you say. But what we're talking about here must then be an assumption because you didn't have any personal knowledge about that, nobody said anything specific about that, and I think that we clarified that in the course of this that nobody ever directly told you that the commander of Operations Group South issued such on order or that you heard about that. Do we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we agree about that and we agreed about that earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you spoke about this before, and I think it's important, so let's confirm it in some way or another. About this: You didn't have any written information, you didn't issue any written information as the security organ to any of your superiors according to that line of security hierarchy. I assume -- you said that you were told that the KOG Sid told you that you should not be involved with that and that somebody else will deal with that. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct you a little bit, Mr. Domazet. I said that on the basis of rumours that were going around among members of the 80th Brigade, and the local population, I wrote to the executive operations group that there were rumours going around about the execution of prisoners from the Vukovar Hospital, that information was going around, that this information was going around about that. And in that sense I received a recommendation from the superior security organ that I should only deal with the security issues in the 80th Brigade, and that others are going to investigate this other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's be specific. It says here that it was reported of the operations group. Did you mean the counter-intelligence group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I made a mistake. Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It went to the KOG in Sid in written form, in one of the daily reports. Not -- not later 24th, 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you've clarified everything. It went to the KOG in Sid, you said, several days after that. So you're talking about the 24th, the 25th. I assume you're thinking of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of what are you told orally, that the KOG in Sid would pick up on that matter, were you later told what was done in this respect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was suggested to me that I should not deal with that, that I should worry about the brigade and not worry about this other job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you don't know if anyone -- if the KOG Sid informed anyone superior to them about this matter.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have access to any such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were talking about the way of communicating by written reports with the KOG in Sid, you wrote about reports that were coded which you personally had to type, because they were strictly confidential, or someone else did that who was authorised to do that and that these reports were delivered by courier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I don't know how to type, the reports were handwritten, but then later when I had some help, my colleagues, officers, would -- or non-commissioned officers would then type the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were talking about making these reports in three copies and that you kept two for yourself, and one copy you, at some point, destroyed and gave one copy to the security of the 24th Corps in Kragujevac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was obliged to write two reports, one for my superior security organs, one for myself, but during visits by security organs, they occasionally asked me for a report in order to complete their -- or justify their visits to the front. When they would arrive, I would give them the reports. Everything that I did not give to them, I took over there. So as a rule I had to always write reports in two copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you destroyed this third copy. When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before leaving Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you have any information about whether these reports are still kept in the archives of the 24th Corps? Because in your statements you frequently said that you do not remember exactly what you wrote but that it's all contained in your reports.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that to the organ chief of the 24th Corps, where that is archived. I don't know where and how it's -- where these documents are and how it's archived, but if you can, you can always check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic perhaps informed about that? Because in a way, he is the superior along that line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic was Deputy Commander of the corps for police matters. And the commander, or rather, the corps chief security -- security organ chief is actually more authorised to cover my work. Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic is in charge of the work of the military police in the 80th Motorised Battalion, and some other units in the corps. You may disagree, but that's how it is; I didn't make this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who is this other commander, this other person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to wait a little bit so I can recall the last name. I, at this moment, I cannot remember. He was also a lieutenant-colonel at the time. Later he was a colonel. Later, perhaps if it comes up, I will -- when it comes up, will tell you the name. It's Lieutenant-Colonel Jovasevic [phoen]. I'm sorry, I needed a little time to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, tell me the following: Since the evening you returned from Ovcara with the two officers, and then for those few days that the Guards Brigade was still there, did you have any opportunity of meeting with Captain Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Karanfilov, but I did see Karan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you would go to Sid, did you find out about a school in Sid by the name of Sremski Front? Are you familiar with this school? Do you know if any organ was located at that school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that. Perhaps if you told me who was supposed to have been stationed there, that might jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I asked a little bit earlier about Captain Karanfilov. We have some information that he was connected to that school, but I thought maybe you would know what period that was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was the security organ in the counter-intelligence group of the Guards Motorised Brigade. That's how he was introduced to me. What the actual situation was, perhaps you can get the book of records of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and everybody's entered there according to their establishment position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was interested in something else. If he had -- I just wanted to know if actually his duties in that line perhaps were in the Sid KOG. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't really tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am nearing the end of my cross-examination, and there's still some time left before the break; however, I would like to take the break now, by your leave, because I seem to have gone quite quickly through my questions and I would like to check my notes and see whether I maybe overlooked some of my questions, or perhaps I can even cut my examination shorter after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the break now then, Mr. Domazet. In view of the progress of time, the Chamber would indicate that it will keep open the prospect of extending the hearing today to be able to finish the witness. It seems now a reasonable prospect of doing that, so that arrangements can be made for that during this break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as promised, I used up the break to cut my examination as short as possible. I only have a few questions left for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My first question is: Was there another KOG active in the territory? You have mentioned something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you anything more specific since there was no cooperation on our part with them. There were several commissioned and non-commissioned officers there, but -- we used to see each other, but there was no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does this mean -- actually, what does it mean when you say there was no cooperation? Does that mean that there was no cooperation between you yourself and them, or between the Sid KOG and them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any cooperation with them. If our superior would instruct us to that effect, we would cooperate, but we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was one of the officers there Major Muncan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but I can't tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were saying something that -- to the effect that at the time the brigade was leaving Negoslavci for Belgrade, and your Motorised Brigade was assuming responsibility for the town, you, as the counter-intelligence and security organ, were given this new assignment which had to do with the Sid KOG. Can you tell us who was it who linked you up with them for this transfer of duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A meeting was called for the entire Operations Group South, which meant that all the security organs were there from the level of the chief of security of brigades down to battalion and independent unit security organs. This was held at Sid in a large cinema hall where we were given our future assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You personally, on behalf of the 80th Motorised Brigade whose security organ you were, you cooperated with them on your tasks that were germane to your expertise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes my cross-examination. But, lastly, I would like to present the view of the Defence for Mr. Mrksic, or rather Mr. Mrksic himself, as regards the meeting with him. He, unfortunately, does not remember you personally, that's to say having seen you there, or the meeting itself, because of the lapse of time and the eventful period. I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber of this. Thank you, Your Honour, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, I would submit that the case should be put clearly whether there was a meeting at that time on the 20th, whether Vojnovic attended that meeting, was there a subsequent meeting with this topic being mentioned with Vojnovic and Vukosavljevic? And it is not, in my submission, appropriate just to say, well, he cannot remember one way or the other. I would submit the case should be put absolutely clearly, so everybody knows where they stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What, Mr. Moore, are you saying has not been done in compliance with the rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am submitting that there is an earlier challenge that should be looked at. That was a challenge, I believe, put to the Witness Trifunovic. My understanding was that Mr. Mrksic was not at Negoslavci for any particular meeting. Now, I cannot from the back of my memory quote exactly word for word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have said enough, Mr. Moore. You have reminded me. If the Defence is maintained that Colonel Mrksic was not at Negoslavci on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991, that should be put to the witness, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on that afternoon, as was customary, a briefing was held where commanders reported to Colonel Mrksic, and it is quite evident. However, as I told the witness, the meeting was held until 1800 hours, because after the meeting, that's to say at 1800 hours, a report was submitted to the 1st Military District as was, in fact, the practice, the daily practice. This report was signed by Colonel Mrksic, and we have it as Exhibit 341, unless I'm mistaken, and I don't believe I am. It's part of the case file. That's how long the meeting lasted, and what happened about it. Now, whether Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was there or not, it's difficult to say. The witness himself does not remember. Had there been mention of this, he would probably remember this. And after that, he left Negoslavci. That's why I insisted on this particular time-frame, and I tried to establish when this conversation took place. If you believe that I need to add anything to that, I will follow the Trial Chamber's instruction; however, I believe that this is enough from the point of view of Mr. Mrksic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand the effect of what you have just said, combined with some cross-examination of an earlier witness, the position may be advanced by your client that he was not in Negoslavci on the evening of the 20th of November, certainly at any of the times suggested by this witness, but that he had, in fact, if I remember, gone to Belgrade. Now, if that is the position of your client, you need to put this to the witness. If it's not your client's position, if he accepts that he could have been at Negoslavci at the times indicated by this witness, which, as you have pointed out in your cross-examination, extend very well beyond 1800 hours, then you should be putting -- you would have no need to put it. But if it is the case that you advance that your client was not at Negoslavci then, then in that case you should raise this matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will proceed in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As was quite evident from my line of questioning, you saw, sir, that I insisted on the timing of the specific events because, I repeat, this particular meeting which was held every day, including the 20th, had to have ended by the 1800 hours, could have lasted perhaps a minute longer, but not more than that. In your statement you state that it was at around 1900 hours or 2000 hours. At that time he was no longer the commander at Negoslavci. He was not at the command, that's to say, at the command at Negoslavci. As you have heard the Honourable Judge, I am duty-bound as the Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic to put this case of ours clearly to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I put this to you: It is a position, as I understand it, advanced by the Defence of Colonel Mrksic that he could not have been at the meeting at Negoslavci at the times you have described in his evidence, and that because he had left Negoslavci very shortly after 6.00 p.m. on the evening of the 20th of November. Now, does that proposition affect your recollection or your evidence in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I stand by my statement. I said clearly that I could not specify the time because of the lapse of time, because of the situation I was in. I stand by what I said, that I informed Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic of the situation as I stated. Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Vojnovic together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And does it remain your evidence that immediately after you and Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic had concluded the meeting with Colonel Mrksic that you then were ordered to go to Ovcara by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and you went directly to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, my name is Borivoje Borovic, and I appear for Mr. Radic. My first question: You stated that the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade was stationed at the Petrova Gora area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it in coordinated action with the other units in the area in the period you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. It was under the Guards Motorised Brigade, within their structure, and I do not know who they acted jointly with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, in what period of time was the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade present at the Petrova Gora area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- can you hear me now? Can you hear me well? It's fine, thank you. The 2nd Infantry Battalion, as far as I remember, was mobilised in late October, early November, perhaps during the last two days of October and the first three days of November, but I believe that the officers of the Guards Motorised Brigade would be more familiar with this and you can find it in the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but you just mentioned the 2nd and we talked about the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I might confuse the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd Infantry Battalions, that's why I will mention the commander, and that's the Captain First Class Lalovic. But as far as I remember, that was the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and the security officer there of that battalion was Tomislav Vukelic, along with Commander Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did I hear you well in saying that in this particular battalion you had your own security officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he report to you from the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the -- rather, no, not for the time he was within the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So when was it that he started reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as he returned to the Battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to tell us the strength of this battalion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had about 2 -- 360, 370 men, but it should have had the full strength of 500 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you the figures as I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The company of the military police commanded by Vezmarovic, did it have the status of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was an independent company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Pursuant to military regulations is it not the status of an independent company to be that of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us talk about the company, the independent company of the military police. It is at the level of a battalion, but the colonel-major would be commander of the battalion, whereas the captain first class would be the commander of the independent company. They are -- hold the same level as do the battalions. That's to say in terms of their superior officers, because their superior is the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that in your ICTY statement you seem to have said that it the status of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could my learned friend, if he's going to make that suggestion, just refer the witness to the passage so that we have a clear perception of it and the witness has a clear perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I respect the rules, and I said "it seems to me," I did not refer the witness to any passage. When the time comes, I'm ready, and I have all the witness's statements, and I also have the English version for the Trial Chamber and the OTP so as to save them time. If I ask the witness to read something, then I will confront the witness with the passage I want him to read and I will provide you with the directions as to where to find that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: One of the witnesses in this trial stated that there was a Desna Supoderica detachment. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say to that when I asked somebody about Leva Supoderica, they said they didn't exist. When I asked about Desna Supoderica, they said they didn't know about that. I don't have any personal knowledge about the Desna Supoderica detachment. I just -- I can just tell you what I heard from other people, and other people told me it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vukovar, what was your task in the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Can you refer me to a specific period?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Vukovar, when you arrived in Vukovar, what was the task of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the last unit in Vukovar. Its battalions, the 1st, the 2nd, and the 3rd, had its deployment, the divisions as well. In practical terms it was the unit stationed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question was very specific: In military terms, where was it stationed? What was the reason why you were sent to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was according to the order of my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you: That was the unit that was deployed in Vukovar, in -- as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me be more specific, then. Was your task to take Vukovar and protect the Serbs in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any such task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now I am going to ask the usher to give you your statements. And since you have authorised your statements in B/C/S by your signature, can you please locate paragraph number 35 in your statement. I never thought that you might dispute this, to be honest, but can you look at paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That is your ICTY statement. Can you please locate paragraph 35. You are a security man, I am sure you will not have a difficult time finding it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, do you know what you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, there is a mistake in transcript. Page 72, line 20, page 71, line 23, I asked about Desna Supoderica and in the transcript the reference is to Leva Supoderica. Let's not dwell upon the transcript. I repeat my question:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a Desna Supoderica detachment in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you are now mixing two or three issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's drop that at the moment. Since your transcript does not reflect what you said, we are going back to that question. Was there a Desna Supoderica detachment in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no such detachment. I didn't know anything of such detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now we go back to paragraph 35, and would you be so kind and read the two first sentences in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I did not have any particular information about the mission of the 80th Motorised Brigade when we were mobilised and sent to the SBZS. I believe we were sent to take Vukovar protect the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does it say here that your task was to protect the Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I understand your question. You're asking me about my arrival in Vukovar on the 23rd and 24th or the 25th, when the 80th Motorised Brigade entered Vukovar. The 80th Brigade did not go to Vukovar as a formation as it was. It was mobilised and all the battalions were resubordinated to other units, if you were listening to me carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We are wasting time here and I did not have any reason to ask you about the 23rd, 24th or 25th of November of 1991. I just asked you about the liberation of Vukovar, what was the task, and now you are moving on to a different topic. Let's go back to paragraph 35. What was your task -- what was the task of the 80th Motorised Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being interrupted all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're not being interrupted all the time, and with the utmost respect, if my learned friend is going to refer to paragraph 35, he should look at the subheading that is immediately above that. It relates to the 15th and 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the paragraph very clearly, but in this paragraph, in this sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Borovic, no need to go into explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the territory, did you have conversations as a security man with the Serbs who were in Croatian prisons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With a number of Serbs who were in Croatian prisons I did have interviews and I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they tell you about the situation that they were confronted with and what their life was in Vukovar during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't talk to many of them, but I did have an opportunity to talk to some people whose names I don't remember. There was a man who was a Serb, and he was the chief of anti-aircraft defence in the municipal staff of Vukovar before the beginning of the war there. He was arrested by the Croatian armed forces and they used him to dig trenches and graves, and as soon as I got his initial information, I handed him over to others who continued working with him and talking to him. People from the command who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 35, which you can now consult, that's why your statement is in front of you, you stated, "When I was in the SBZS, I talked to some Serbs who had spent some time in Croatian prisons." You mention a number of Serbs. What did they tell you, how did they perceive the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their prison time was very difficult. There was ill-treatment, they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any killings in the Croatian prisons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any such information. Nobody told me that. This person that I mentioned told me that he had fared badly, he was psychologically disturbed, and as soon as I heard that, I handed him over to the organs in my superior command who continued working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar, did you come by documents written by Jastreb, the commander of ZNG?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally get in contact with those documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the letter that he sent to Tudjman in which he says that if he didn't send help, the situation would repeat in Zagreb. We also seized his radio set. It was an American-made radio set, and I ordered the code to be broken in, but the superior command did not deem that necessary. There are also some other documents, but it is very difficult to now remember all of them and list all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find in these documents confirmation on the need to protect the Serbs in the JNA -- the Serbs in Vukovar by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That there was a need for the JNA to protect the Serbs in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't find that, or maybe I don't remember finding anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 35 again, and can you read the last sentence in that paragraph. Can you read the four last lines, starting with, "Our military police ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Our military police found documents signed by Croatian military commander Mile Dedakovic when they got into former Croatian headquarters, located in a cellar. Those documents confirmed the information about the need to protect the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't understand you. What are you saying? Are you saying that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I signed the page. Those documents confirm the information about the need to protect the Serbs. I did sign the statement, I don't have any doubt about that, but I don't remember any documents expressing the need to protect the Serbs. I did sign the statements, but I apologise, I didn't -- I don't know, this must have been a slip. I don't know how I authorised this, because I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you receive information that Serbs were threatened in Vukovar before you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did receive that. And it says that in paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally visit the area called Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When and why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there on several occasions. That's where one of my battalions under the command of Captain First Class Lasovic [phoen] was deployed, and I visited and contacted all the battalions, including that one, sometimes on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the battalion was there in October and November, as you said a while ago?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that it I had some 400 to 500 men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that according to its formation, it should have had 499 men. At that time 500 people was the strength of battalions. At that time I believe that they had under -- somewhat under 400 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you ever hear that Captain Miroslav Radic participated in any evacuation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions you visited Ovcara, you were in Ovcara. Yesterday you said it was around 1700 hours, and I accept that, and you also stated yesterday and today and in various statements that we are not going to go through, that you found Captain Vezmarovic there when you got there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed today that in the operative log of the 80th Motorised Brigade it says that the military police company withdrew at 2230.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, do you agree with me when I say that Captain Vezmarovic spent at least five and a half hours in the hangars, if he was there at 1700 hours and if it says in the log that they withdrew at 2230?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the times in the log are correct. In my view, there is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A mistake that was slight?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been more than half an hour discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Even if there is a half an hour discrepancy, does that mean that Captain Vezmarovic must have spent at least five hours there before you found him there in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the military police company went to Ovcara on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who could have issued an order for them to go to Ovcara to provide security for the prisoners who were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Captain Vezmarovic, you mean? It could have been only the brigade commander, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That was Colonel Vojnovic, wasn't that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your statements you described the vehicles that you used to go to Ovcara on the first occasion, as well as on the second occasion. In one of the statements you say that your second departure was sometime after 2100 hours, but that is not important. You also mentioned that you were in a Campagnola vehicle when you went there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the 80th Motorised Brigade had, on its fleet, those Campagnola vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had in the brigade command and in the communications company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact, do you know whether with that group of prisoners the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade arrived in Ovcara, together with that group of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you know [as interpreted], but that may have been the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, that is what this could mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The second time you went to Ovcara you said to the investigators of the OTP that you found there about 200 to 300 people. Yesterday you said that there could have been even more people, over 300 people altogether; however, in the statement that you have before you under number 3, the statement that you gave before the Belgrade court, to the question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that there were over 60 of them. 60 members of the Territorial Defence, and locals. Would you accept that you said that in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Page 16.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: English version, page 23. Did you find it? The Presiding Judge, question. Can you please check whether I have provided you with the correction information and that is that you stated before the Trial Chamber there that there were over 60 members of TO and local population at Ovcara when you arrived there for the second time, and before you returned from there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said before, that there were over 300 people, that is the realistic picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. But does it say here in the statement that you mentioned the figure of 60?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic tell you at any time that on the 20th of November he was at Ovcara? Do you have knowledge of that? And if you do, what time was he there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have had an opportunity now of locating what my learned friend has been putting to the witness. And, in fairness to the witness, my learned friend has not put the question to him from the Presiding Judge, and it is the Presiding Judge who actually numbers or names the number, and asks the question, "Does that mean there were over 60 of them?" The answer was, "It was definitely over 60, now I am not [sic] giving a number." It was a result of a question where the number is given. He is not saying himself that he estimates 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resolve that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't think that this was in dispute. Please take your statement. I provided the entire statement deliberately. I am going to read and you can follow so everybody can see where we are. "Witness Dragi Vukosavljevic: If -- so when you don't have the balance of power, 1:3, then the situation is slipping out of control and you cannot control it. These are the regulations. "Presiding Judge: And if there are 20 of you and ten of them, that is one to three to whose advantage? 1:3 the advantage of the forces who are carrying out something? ... I'm not sure if I understand." "When you don't have the balance of power 1:3, then the situation is slipping out of control and you cannot control it. These are the regulations. "Presiding Judge: And if there are 20 of you and 10 of them, then it is 1:3 to whose advantage? The advantage of the forces who are carrying out something, 1:3. "Witness Dragi Vukosavljevic: You see, if. "Presiding Judge: I'm not sure that I understand. "Witness Dragi Vukosavljevic: If you are securing, you could be three times weaker and carry out the task of defence and security poorly, but if you have to intervene and do something, then you have to be three times stronger. That is the basic rule in the army. "Presiding Judge: What now? On the basis of this we are trying to establish how many members of the Territorial Defence were there, people from Vukovar. If there were 20 of your men, does it mean that there were over 60 of them? So the ratio was 1:3? "Witness Dragi Vukosavljevic: It was definitely over 60. Now I'm giving a number." And you didn't provide a number. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did give a number, but you are taking the thing out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did I read everything correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention in that statement the figure of 300 people or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. We would have to read the whole thing to see if I said that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I did read the whole statement, perhaps if my learned friend the Prosecutor found any information that you mentioned the figure of 300 people at the Belgrade Ovcara trial, I will accept that without hesitation. Do you know Jovan Novkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called him Joca. But there was no special nickname. In some lists he is mentioned as Joca Kafic. I knew him as Joca, he was a morale person in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he (redacted) assistance for morale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the persons who had the legal authority to initiate legal proceedings in the event of criminal acts being committed in the area that he was in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the assistant commander for morale in a battalion has that right. As for the same function in the artillery battalion, I don't know. The deputy -- the assistant commander of the commander for morale is at the same time the assistant for legal affairs. I don't know if that is the same in an artillery battalion, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your modest knowledge, as you describe it, is he as a morale person duty-bound -- or assistant for morale, duty-bound to send a report to his chief of morale in case a grave crime is committed, and he established that it was so, in the area where he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You were at Ovcara on two occasions. We're now talking about that time you arrived there at dusk, at around 1700 hours. The question is: Did you see, in that brief period of time, any liquidations in the hangar or in front of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see some groups of people being taken away somewhere from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a large pit in front of the entrance to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At 2100 hours and on, until 2230 hours, in that period of time did you see any corpses in front of the hangar, in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear in that period of time, which was from 1700 hours to 2230 hours or before 1700 hours, did you notice any liquidations, people being taken away for executions, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the whole question. There was something about units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you came --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the interpreters did not catch the whole question, I'm going to repeat my question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the 80th Motorised Brigade- and I'm first of all thinking of the military police company - in the period before 1700 hours when they were there and in the period after that, from 1700 until 2230 hours, tell you that there were any liquidations or any people being taken away for execution or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody told me anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, at any point in time, notice an excavator in front of the hangar entrance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please speak up.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice in that period that there was a tractor in front of the hangar entrance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now a more general question: When you were in Vukovar, did you know where the headquarters was, where the operation to liberate Vukovar was being executed from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no; which staff, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of headquarters or staff overseeing the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Guards Motorised Brigade staffs, and they were in charge of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And where was this staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please kindly tell us what a staff is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean what is a staff or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What constitutes a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Headquarters or a staff is the command part of any unit. The first staff would appear at the unit at the level of a company or a brigade, and then later -- and also light artillery battalion. And later you would have it in the regiment a brigade division. So a staff or a headquarters is that part of a unit that controls and commands the services and branches in any given unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said something, but I don't want to dispute that at this moment. But my question is: What is the first establishment formation unit that would form a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A headquarters does not have a headquarters, it has an observation force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that you were the first person besides the Prosecutor to say that the komandir of a company is the first person to have a headquarters, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the command of a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that is not a staff in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military sense, it's called the company command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But not a staff or a headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the end would we agree that a battalion is the first organisational unit to have a staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right. You are right about the company command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I am right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the lawyers would appear to know something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor is not right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise about the comment, but I will continue. This is in the spirit of my communication with my learned friend from the Prosecution and I hope he won't take it ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that you recollected about talking with the commander of Ovcara, the local commander of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for a moment I would like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftic came to assist you, although he was charged with the police at a certain point in time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the question whether he came to assist me; yes, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that in the period starting with the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say it was after the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he in Vukovar on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you base your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary for you to see him upon his arrival or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it would have been proper for us to meet. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the Vukovar events, as the security officer there, did you follow the work of the journalists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that much, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what you know of it, to the extent you dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall meeting or seeing a journalist at the time. I am not sure what you are referring to specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
