utterances.text: For the duration of war operations in the areas you toured and at the Negoslavci headquarters, did you see journalists reporting on the events and were you in touch with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I believe there was a schoolmate of mine, Jovic, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which newspaper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was magazine Svetlost, from Kragujevac, and he was a schoolmate of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us finish. At the time of the events at Ovcara it is the Defence case that the local commander of Ovcara was (redacted) from the 80th Motorised Brigade. With him there was his unit too. As well as the assistant for morale who was, to a certain extent, duty-bound to launch investigations into war crimes if any are committed. Initially there was a military police company there from -- which means on the 18th and the 20th. You were there as chief of security with your two officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with two of my officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: With two officers who were accompanying you when you came at Ovcara, and there was also Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, who stated so himself. My question to you is as follows: All of you from the 80th Motorised Brigade who were there, and in view of the fact that the first and the second time you arrived at Ovcara you stated that you did not notice members of the Guards Motorised Brigade --

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: -- am I right in saying that you too incur some responsibility and the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean I personally, or the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I mean the 80th Motorised Brigade and its commander. Perhaps those who are most responsible for not taking any action, because after 2230 hours, when you were no longer there, very serious crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the commander acted within his chain of command, that he could not be held responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is one point that I overlooked during the examination by Mr. Borovic. Mr. Borovic mentioned paragraph 35, where the last sentence says the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. I have finished my cross-examination, and now you seem to be going back to that. What is it that you want to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that you misled me with your question in the following way: It says that: "These documents confirm the information about the need to protect the Serbs." You brought this into the following context, if I understood you well. That the HVO, that's to say Dedakovic provided a document with a view to protecting the Serbs. I'm standing by what I said before. These documents confirm the information about the need to protect the Serbs, and this refers to the documents we found in Dedakovic's staff, because in those documents one could see that there was a threat to the Serbs. I did not have any specific information on the mission of the brigade, I merely stated that this was with a view to protecting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please not interrupt each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that none of what the witness has read was, in fact, entered into the transcript because he read it too quickly. Could you please slow down. There was nothing misleading there. Can you tell us what the problem is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you, Mr. Borovic, to have put to me that in this paragraph 35 that the Croats had the intention to protect the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically, the documents found in the headquarters of Mile Dedakovic pointed to the need for the JNA to protect the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. I put the question to you quite clearly, and your answer was clear. There was no misunderstanding there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Borovic. I really misunderstood you, and I wanted to rectify any possible mistake that might have been entered into the transcript. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this completes it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have ordered redactions of the name of the protected witness in the cross-examination. Mr. Lukic. Oh, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to receive your instruction as to our further proceeding, because we are due to sit longer. Perhaps because of the interpreters and the other staff, we should decide when we have the break. I can proceed, and I believe I shall take some hour to one hour 15 minutes, roughly. Now, perhaps, we should decide on the breaks we are going to have for the benefit of the interpreters and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am pleased to assist you. We will sit for -- until five minutes to 2.00, or a slightly earlier time if that's a convenient break. We will then have an hour break for lunch. And we can then sit for one further session only, which will be the completion of your cross-examination and Mr. Moore's re-examination. So your estimate of time of just over an hour, will be excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my part, I will do my best, Your Honours, to follow your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukosavljevic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Not that well, but I'm sure we will overcome the problem eventually. My name is Momcilo Bulatovic, and I am one of the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin, and on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin, I will be putting questions to you. I will do my best to make my questions brief and clear, and I appeal to you to do the same in answering my questions, which will ensure your speedy return home. I kindly ask you to make a slight pause before answering my questions so that we avoid overlapping. This will be of assistance for the interpreters and will make sure the transcript that Their Honours will use will be accurate. Mr. Vukosavljevic, we had occasion to hear the jobs you did, and what it was you did in the army. These duties you had, and the scope of activities of the security organs, was this governed by the rules of service of the security organs of the then armed forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, by those rules as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These rules, did they govern the scope and activities of the security organs, including the command and control of these organs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I used or had occasion to consult these rules was in 1999 when I was mobilised for some three months. I would not be able to tell you anything specific about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From your memory - we want to save time and not have you read the rules now - having had work -- having worked as a security officer for a long time, could you tell us and the Trial Chamber some of the basic duties of the security officer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that, and I said that these were mostly counter-intelligence activities and -- and the rest is secret, so I wouldn't be able to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony here you talked of the position of the security organ in the establishment units. You spoke of your brigade, the 80th Motorised Brigade, and you stated how many battalions it had, and that it had security officers there as well, and what the relationship was. My question is, this structure, was it governed by the rules, and was it the same type of structure in other units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. As far as the 130th Motorised Brigade was concerned, which was under the 24th Corps, the structure of that battalion was identical to ours; however, there were other units, like tank units, PVO units, and so on and so forth. It depended on the manpower they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit 107 on the monitor, please. This is the entire document, that is the rule of service of the security organ. Could we have page 16. The ERN number is 0090-9825. That's right. Thank you. Could we please have item 16 zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it clearly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see if this can be done. Mr. Vukosavljevic, can you see item 16 of the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out paragraph 16, and then I will have a couple of questions for you. "The security organ is immediately subordinated to the commanding officer of the command unit, institution or staff of the armed forces within which establishment it is contained, and shall be answerable for its -- for his work to that particular commanding officer whereas the security organs of the JNA in the organisations for the NVO shall be held answerable to the competent assistant to the federal secretary for national defence." Have I read this out accurately, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for us now, what does this part mean, that the security organ shall be immediately subordinated to the commanding officer of the command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my case, that meant that I was directly subordinated to the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the security organ has no command role whatsoever in the unit of which it is part.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the two officers there who were with me in the staff, in my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could we see ERN page -- that's page 12 of the rules, the ERN number being 0090-9823 on the monitor. I apologise, that's page 13 of the rules. On page 13 we have subparagraph d). Could we have that part zoomed in, or can you see that, Mr. Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out. It is part of paragraph 7, that's 7 d), it says: "The security organs shall participate in commanding in the professional sense over the units of the military police."

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I was looking at the other d), which means collecting and checking data for operational needs of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have this on the monitor. It's item 7 on page 12, that's where it -- item 7 starts, and then we're looking at the subpart d), which is contained on page 13. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I can see that, in commanding in the professional sense over the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The security organs participate in the command, in the professional command of the units of military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may intervene and make a correction in the transcript. This is what we discussed a few days ago. Professional command and control. The interpreters now, on page 98/23, the word used is "command" although we have an official translation in which in the English in paragraph 2, it says performing specialist, and I had to intervene in that sense. This is what we discussed earlier on, the difference between command and control, and the special aspects of the two, which are very specific in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would have appreciated if they had been given an official translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have heard that, Mr. Lukic. The interpreters are translating in the ordinary flow of language as it happens. If you want to ensure that some very specific approach is taken, it's in your hands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask you, Mr. Vukosavljevic, since you have provided us with a lot of professional explanation about the relationship between the security organ and the military police, which is a relationship which is very important here because we are trying to establish what that relationship contains and how it functions on the ground, and now you have heard about the difference in terminology and -- and how confusions may arise. Could you please try and explain, what is the role and function of the security organ vis-a-vis the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm professional enough to provide you with that explanation because these tasks and these jobs concerning the professional guidance was something that Colonel Jeftic did, and he came to assist me, and in that professional sense I wouldn't be able to tell you much more in addition to what it says in the rules of service, in which it says that the security organ coordinates, they do not command, the units of the military police. You will see that if you go back, and you will see that the security organs do not command over the military police units. They can provide guidance, they can coordinate, but not command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, we can agree that there is no situation in which a security organ could issue any orders or instructions to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; in my knowledge, that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that one of the jobs and tasks of a security organ is to participate in providing security for high state officials, foreign heads of state, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. I know that the duty of the security organ of a brigade is provide security for the brigade commander. And anything beyond that is beyond the scope of my knowledge or authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you anything about that, but with regard to what we have just discussed and what you have spoken about, I'm going to ask you one more thing. An officer of the organ of security who has professional duty towards the military police but does not have a command role vis-a-vis military police, does he propose to the commander of the unit, institution, and so on so forth, how to use units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if that proposal is asked from him. Or he can do it of his own accord if he feels the need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, we have stated that this is what the rules say and that the rules are there to be implemented. Will the two of us agree that the rules were what they were, and that the procedure was what it was, and that you followed that procedure in your capacity as a security organ, and this is exactly what was followed in practice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, theory and practice should overlap, should be one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now we shall move on to the developments that we are interested in here. Let's start with a bit of a technical introduction, although you have provided us with a lot of technical details. You said that the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade was an independent company.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an independent company of the military police. And it differed from the military police companies that are on the strength of any of the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the difference to me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what the military police company of the 80th Brigade looked like, and I can repeat, although I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two battalion -- it had two squads. One was the traffic squad. It had a service department for the commander. And those squads consisted of 10 people. Those were younger people who were lower-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that your answer has not been recorded properly on page 101, line 24. Mr. Vukosavljevic, I would kindly ask you to speak slowly and to repeat the strength and the composition of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the company of the military police of the 80th Brigade was as follows: The first and the second police squad, there were two platoons; there was one traffic platoon, there was a department for services. There was a commander of the platoon and platoon officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the company commander had his deputy; and if he did, who was it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the establishment, I don't think that there was a Deputy Commander in the -- in the company. I may be mistaken. My memory may be jogged with some documents. However, in principle, a Deputy Commander is the commander of the first police platoon. It can be somebody else if that is according to the commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was Captain Vezmarovic's superior officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Captain Vezmarovic could only be issued orders by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There was nobody else --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 102 of the transcript, line 25 -- actually 23, the answer should have been recorded, the answer provided by the witness to my question whether Captain Vezmarovic could be issued orders by anybody else but Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, and the witness said, "That is correct." The answer has not been recorded. If you want me to clarify this with the witness, I shall do so. If not, maybe we can agree that this answer is recorded the way I have just said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that the answer couldn't be heard. That being the answer, please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I will try to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, during your testimony, during the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination by my colleagues, we have dealt with a number of things. I may have to go over some of the ground again, and I have to ask you again. There was no way that Captain Vezmarovic could be issued an order by a security officer, either from the 80th Motorised Brigade, the Guards Brigade, or any other establishment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A security officer can, if he is issued an order to convey an order to Captain Vezmarovic, but this is the order of the brigade commander. The brigade commander can also send that order by communication means, by courier, but the order that is issued to the commander of the military police has to come from the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we would all benefit from that. Especially the interpreters and those supporting us. We will resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Judge Van den Wyngaert is not sitting this afternoon. The other two judges have resolved to continue the hearing under the rule. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, Mr. Vukosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned security officers of the security organ, namely Mr. Karanfilov and Mr. Karan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you were particularly in touch with Mr. Karan and you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If -- it must be a misinterpretation, because security officers of the security organ, they are security officers of the Guards Brigade actually, are they not? Important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is a matter of contention. There is enough that they are security officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] I did not wish to state at any moment that Mr. Karan and Mr. Karanfilov were not officers of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, you said that you had rare contacts with Mr. Karan on a professional basis, that you exchanged information through two written reports, if I understood it correctly, and the rest was just oral exchange of specialist information. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understand what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that Captain Karan, as the security officer of the Guards Motorised Brigade covered, in terms of security, the units at the rear post of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the security organ decides himself on the engagement of his security officers. I can tell you how I myself acted when using the services of my security officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm merely asking whether you allow for this possibility, since you yourself gave assignments to your security officers, and you said that the -- Mr. Karan would cover certain duties.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a matter for his chief to decide upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you met Mr. Sljivancanin, you described this encounter, and you said that he referred you to his officers, professional associates, with whom you were supposed to exchange information. Do you recall at the time of meeting Mr. Sljivancanin for the first time telling -- that he told you that Mr. Karan was the competent security officer and that he was his assistant for counter-intelligence and that's why he referred you to cooperate with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me that -- or he didn't have any need to refer me to him. He didn't tell me of his title. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had cooperation with Mr. Karan. Can you tell us what sort of cooperation that was. Was it correct or was there mutual respect and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you what the elements of the 80th Motorised Brigade were. The security information concerning the Motorised Brigade were not the same as when the brigade was up to full strength. That's why this cooperation was not quite extensive. As far as our personal relationship was concerned, well, Mr. Karan was quite forthcoming; he offered whatever equipment he had at his disposal for me to use, like the telephone services, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, insofar as you cooperated, the cooperation was quite correct and proper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Danilovic as the person who -- or rather, Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic - I apologise - who led the operation at Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for us what this -- the conducting of the operation on his part involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic was the chief of the staff of the 80th Brigade, and in the absence of the military police company, the commander opted for him, and also because he was reliable. That is why he deployed the forces and gave them assignments for security. And both him and I observed and controlled the way the action was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, during your testimony here, you explained why you were present at Ovcara between the 18th and the 19th of November, that it was, in fact, in order to oversee the action.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the duties inherent to my post as a member of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the overseeing itself, the monitoring, included.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It included the control or supervision of both the internal and external security, the supervision of the soldiers, and it was all within my regular line of duty. There wasn't anything exceptional or extraordinary about it, requiring any exceptional action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to mislead anyone, my question concerning Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic and yourself had to do with the security of the Mitnica group at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where Lieutenant-Colonel Dan --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It does not involve Ovcara itself.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In one part of your testimony you stated that at some point Mr. Karanfilov arrived and handed the members of the Croatian forces from Mitnica over, and that there was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Danilovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Vojnovic was lieutenant-colonel at the time. He was brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question was not entered into the transcript. My -- that's why I will repeat the question slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At Ovcara on the 18th in the afternoon, there were Mr. Vukosavljevic; Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Brigade, Motorised Brigade; Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. All of them were together when Mr. Karanfilov arrived, and handed these prisoners over to them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mr. Karanfilov said, if anything, who he talked with, and what his role was, as well as how long he stayed there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about this already in my testimony here, and if you want me to, I can repeat what I stated. I can't repeat it word for word, but at any rate he arrived with the group, he talked to us, and to the commander of the Mitnica group, Mr. Filip Karaula. He said that there would be separate rooms for him and his officers, and a separate room for the troops. We offered him food, and he only asked to be given water for his soldiers. We billeted them at one part of Ovcara. There was a rope that was pulled up, and then he left. I didn't hear much of the conversation, because he spoke with Lieutenant-Colonels Danilovic and Vojnovic more than with me, and I am not privy to their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me how long Karanfilov stayed there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you that. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After the evening on the 18th, did you see Mr. Karanfilov again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I used to see him at the command and in the general area, but these were not official contacts. We merely said hello to each other in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you specifically: Do you remember, before leaving Ovcara on the 19th, seeing Mr. Karanfilov at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I told you that I had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Karanfilov at Ovcara on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Vukosavljevic, who sent the military police company of the 80th Brigade and elements of the commanding personnel to go to Ovcara on the 20th in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the security provided to the group from the hospital? The brigade commander. It must have been the brigade commander who did that. But there were no commanding officers, save the two officers who were with me, because the men there were members of the police and the army, as far as I was able to see when I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we see Exhibit 371 on the monitor. This is the operative log. And can we see an entry for the 20th of November at 1600 hours. We would like to use that in order to confirm that we have just heard from the witness. The entry for the 20th of November, please. At the very bottom of that page, under 1600 hours, can this be zoomed in, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the entry in the operative log?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a copy, which is not very legible. Maybe your eyes are better, maybe you can read better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I can see the commander of the brigade asked for the shifts of officers to be defined in order to provide security for the ZNG soldiers and MUP members, and the command officers were designated for that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is part of the operative log that pretty much conforms to what you explained.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a log that was with the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you about the 18th and the meeting, i.e., a chance meeting that you had with Mr. Karanfilov and the time that you spent together there. With regard to that meeting on the 18th at Ovcara in the afternoon hours, I am interested in one thing only: Did you hear that Karanfilov had issued any orders to Vezmarovic or did you hear that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic had issued any orders to Captain Vezmarovic to the effect that in the future all the orders would be issued to him by Mr. Karanfilov? Can you just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. -- Are you referring to the time when the group from Mitnica was guarded?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the Mitnica group was guarded on the 18th of November, 1991, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest ranking officer was Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, and he was in charge of the operation. If the commander said that, the only person he could have said it to was Lieutenant-Colonel Danilovic, not a commander of the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher to provide you with the copies of this document. I'm going to be putting questions to the witness, I am going to be confronting him with certain evidence, and that's why I would like the Prosecutor to have that. The witness already has the statements, this is for the Trial Chamber and for the Prosecution. And this is the statement for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, on the 19th in the morning until the 20th of November, 1991, in the morning when you left Ovcara, until the 20th of November of the same year when, pursuant to the order by Colonel Vojnovic, when you left to -- when you went to Ovcara, did you have any contact with the security organ of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. We may have visited each other, we may have exchanged information. I'm probably -- did because that was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you did have any contacts, were -- was there anything within the scope of that exchange of your specialist information that was different, that could have struck you as unusual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing special that happened or was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You returned after the meeting in the brigade command, the command of the Guards Brigade, you returned to Ovcara, and you were with your driver, as you have already said, and you had left the two officers behind, the ones who were with you the first time around.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 20th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You confused me on the dates. You switched between the dates quite often, so I have to be sure. Yes, I did go with my driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that when you arrived you found the situation as it was and there were more chaos than at the time when you left.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us that you saw three Pinzgauer vehicles that were ready to go back towards Negoslavci, that's how they were facing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the military police were there? The military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade, how many of them were there in Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991, the second time when you went there; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number was the same as the first time, but I don't know what the number was. It was a long time ago. Maybe Vezmarovic would be better suited to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You testified before the judge of the Novi Sad court, Mr. Alimpic, the investigating judge of the Novi Sad court. I believe that the statement is before you. And you said at one point that -- in B/C/S version this is on page 2, and in the English version it is also on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can just bear with me for a moment, Your Honours. Actually, this is page 4, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in the English version it is page 4. The statement was given on the 20th of July before the investigating judge in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Vukosavljevic: "When I returned there in order to convey the message to Captain Vezmarovic, the situation was even more delicate than before. The police had been pushed behind the hangar and were standing by the vehicles." And then you continue to say -- can you explain this: If the police had been pushed behind the hangar and were standing by the vehicles, how can you say that they were ready to leave, that the vehicles were ready to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me the same thing that the judge in Belgrade asked me. This was not behind the hangar, they were actually leaving the hangar to go towards the vehicles. They were not the behind the hangar, as it says here. This is just a mistake, a typing mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will allow that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one letter more than it should be, so hence the mistake. The troops were not behind the hangar, they were coming from the hangar towards the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You went to convey the message to Mr. Vezmarovic, the order that had been issued to him by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And the order was that the troops of the 80th Motorised Brigade should withdraw from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you were supposed to convey to Vezmarovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that you are not sure, because of the situation at hand, that you ever did that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was already in the process of doing whatever he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: When you arrived there, did you see anybody, any of the officers close to Vezmarovic, who might have issued him with an order to withdraw from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Save for the three of us; myself and the chief and the chief of HBAO [as interpreted], there were no other officers that I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the chief of artillery and the chief of ABHO, but they could not have issued such an order to Captain Vezmarovic. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, they couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Will you then allow a possibility, Mr. Vukosavljevic, that you are the one who conveyed the order to Captain Vezmarovic, because it is so obvious that nobody else was there and we heard from you that he did not have any communication means, that he could not communicate with the staff in any other way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, what I told you I'm not sure that I am right, because he was already in the middle of the operation of evacuation that I was supposed to tell him about. They had already been packing, they had already been getting ready to get into the vehicles, and there was no need for me to convey any messages or orders and that's why I told you that I cannot tell you anything exact after such a long time. In practical terms he was already doing what I was supposed to tell him to do. He was already acting according to the message that I was supposed to convey, the order that I had been given for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, we have information in the operative log that it had been ordered to the military police company to go to Ovcara. You have explained who it was who was the only person that could have issued such an order to Captain Vezmarovic. Could Captain Vezmarovic abandon that place and abort the task of his own accord, the task that was given to him by his superior? Could he withdraw from Ovcara without anybody's orders, of his own will?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if he wanted to break the military rules, that was the only way he could have done it. Otherwise, there was no way for him to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You had an occasion to talk to Captain Vezmarovic after all the developments that took place in 1991 -- between 1991 and 2003.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we spoke about this only after we provided our respective testimonies before the court in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the statement you gave to Judge Alimpic. This is page 3. Page 3 of B/C/S, and fourth page of the English version. Let me read to you one segment of the statement that you gave. It reads: "I never spoke to Captain Vezmarovic about this. It was only in April, 2003, when I spoke to the authorised personnel of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, and when they asked me about Captain or Lieutenant Karanfilov, who was an active officer in the Guards Brigade, that I practically learned from the police officers that he had maybe passed along the order to Captain Vezmarovic."

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that Vezmarovic never told you that Karanfilov either issued an order to him or conveyed an order to him and that you only learned about the fact from the police officers during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I spoke about that with Captain Vezmarovic once again about that, after the statement, that -- when I gave the statement to The Hague Tribunal in 2003, and after I gave the statement I spoke to him and he told me, I don't remember everything at Ovcara that night, but thank you very much for having told the investigators that there -- an order had indeed been issued for me to withdraw. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, does this mean that we can conclude that you cannot rule out the possibility that members of the military police and the troops of the 80th Motorised Brigade were getting ready to withdraw at the time when you got there and that they were actually waiting someone to convey this to them, and that perhaps you were the one who did so, owing to the fact that you had left behind two officers who had been there with you on the first occasion, and who knew where and why you were going to the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, I tend to give another explanation. Vezmarovic had probably already received an order from someone before I got there. In other words, I think that this option is more acceptable to me as the security organ. This is more likely, in other words, this version that he -- rather than the version where he would have left the hangar without actually receiving an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, I asked you whether there were any commanding officers there, and whether there was anyone who could issue such an order. You said that Vezmarovic was there and you said that there were no commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not in my presence. But whether there had been someone, as Mr. Vezmarovic is claiming, while I wasn't there, and this is something that Mr. Vezmarovic did say, he said this to me also in 2003, he was very certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you left Ovcara together, according to the log, around 2200 hours and 35 minutes. It could have been a little earlier, but that's not really relevant. What I would like to know is something else. After your return, did you talk to Vezmarovic? Did you have -- did you go to the command to submit a report? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the command, to the brigade commander, and I reported to him. I said that I had conveyed his order, and that -- and I returned to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was Captain Vezmarovic present during this reporting of yours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that it was Captain Vezmarovic's duty to report on a mission accomplished, or on the implementation of an order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe he had done so, but not in my presence. This is something that you should check with Mr. Vezmarovic and Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I was very careful, and I looked through all these statements that you've given, Mr. Vukosavljevic. There is the statement to the investigating judge of the district court in Novi Sad, and then the statement with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal of 18th and 19th July. Then there was your testimony before the special court in Belgrade on the 24th of November, 2004, and I would like to ask you about it. I would like to ask you about something that I have found as a red line through all these statements, and I found it very interesting. It is my impression that when you spoke about this in your testimonies and talked about your conveying the orders to Captain -- to Mr. Vezmarovic, to Captain Vezmarovic, that you actually had some sort of reserve in this area, that you weren't quite open. Am I right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now take a look at the statement to the -- to the representatives of The Hague Tribunal. Have you found it? I'm looking at paragraph 64 of this statement. So this is your statement, and you've signed it, so there is no reason to doubt what's -- what is stated there, because you have signed it. What it says is the following. I will not read the whole paragraph, because I don't think it's relevant, but it says the following: "If Captain Vezmarovic, commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade, was sincere with me about the order, the order which was conveyed to him by Lieutenant Karanfilov ..." et cetera, "the security organ in the Guards Motorised Brigade to withdraw the military police from Ovcara and hand over the prisoners ..." et cetera, et cetera, no need to read the rest. What I'd like to ask you is, where does this question come from, your question, if Captain Vezmarovic was sincere? What is it that makes you doubt his sincerity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question. I have no problems with the question being asked if the whole sentence is read to the witness. But my learned friend is just -- I will use the phrase selecting beneficial passages. The whole part must be read, surely, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is reading it, Mr. Moore. I think we can let him deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Your Honour, do we not need it for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want it for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If you would, please, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Well, I'll read the whole sentence again, and I'm not going to read the whole paragraph, but just the relevant sentence. Whether it is useful, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The paragraph, Mr. Bulatovic. Would you like me to give you a break and I'll read it? "If Captain Vezmarovic, commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade, was sincere with me about the order, which was conveyed to him by Lieutenant Karanfilov, the security organ in the Guards Motorised Brigade, to withdraw the military police from Ovcara and hand over the prisoners to the armed local Serbs, Colonel Mile Mrksic, commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade, should have obviously responded differently based on the information provided to him by Colonel Milorad Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and me. Mrksic had at his disposal the Guards Motorised Brigade, including two military police battalions, to do something. Mrksic was better informed about what was going on than we were. Commanders are kept informed so they can decide on a further course of action."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vukosavljevic, you heard this. My question is, why or wherefor this if he was sincere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt his sincerity at all. Simply I used that word. I could have used some other word. And my reservations with regard to the sincerity of Captain Vezmarovic is non-existent. It could have said there whether it was correct. In other words, that sentence could have been worded differently. I mean, you're stressing this, and I don't quite understand why. There were no reservations at all on my part with regard to Mr. Vezmarovic and, as I've said, after all these years -- after 12 years, he said to me in this context, thank you for saying that it was the commander who ordered the withdrawal of the unit because I had no cover. This was another -- this provided another cover for me. And as for Karanfilov on that night, I did not see him that night [as interpreted]. And the fact that you are insisting on this term -- let me just read that one more time -- the term "sincere," it could have said something else there, to be quite honest. There was nothing, no reservations between me and Captain Vezmarovic, in Vukovar or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic. I kept thinking it was Mr. Bulatovic that was speaking, and I couldn't see him speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but I had to intervene. I think that the reply to the previous question was not correctly related in the -- in the transcript. Perhaps the witness was a bit too fast, so some sentences just got scrambled up. I mean the portion on page 120, from lines 9 to 22. And specifically, it relates to what Mr. Vezmarovic said to the witness in respect of Captain Karanfilov. I think the meaning is not correct in the transcript. And my learned colleague could perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be good enough to indicate to Mr. Bulatovic what your problem is. You can do it privately, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 120, lines 18 and 19. Where it says, "And about Karanfilov that night, I did not see him." That's what it says in the transcript. But I believe the witness did not say that, not for that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether -- I take it you are not able to read the English transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's recorded that your answer said there were no reservations by you about Mr. Vezmarovic, that he said to you in this context, "Thank you for saying it was the commander who ordered the withdrawal of the unit because I had no cover. This provided another cover for me." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But I also said that he told me that Karanfilov had ordered this, had issued this order to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So let's go back again. At the beginning of my cross-examination we discussed the position and status of Mr. Karanfilov, and that it was out of the question - and you confirmed this - that he would issue any orders. So my question to you is: Did you ask Vezmarovic - you, as the security officer - how it was and under what rules he was issued an order or had been issued an order by someone who had no authority to do so and to -- and that he actually implemented that order, executed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss this with Vezmarovic, I never asked him this. Because according to what he believes and in his knowledge, the security organs are his superiors. That is his position, his opinion. But I understood him to mean something else, that Borce Karanfilov had informed him that he should withdraw the unit. That was how I understood what he said to me. Otherwise, I just need to say that the security organ had no authority, could not issue any orders to the military police. And what I understood Dragan Vezmarovic to say was that he had been informed by him and that he had just acted on this order. I did not go into polemics with him about this. There is a slight difference of approach between the two of us on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something: Is Captain Vezmarovic an untrained or insufficiently trained officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say anything about that. You should read his -- the assessment of his work and perhaps you can find it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now take a look at the statement given to the investigating judge of the district court in Belgrade on page 9. Page 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's page 9 in the B/C/S version. Under item 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. I'll find it. I'm sure we're all working in the interests of justice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th line from the top, the sentence begins with, "I returned to Ovcara."

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just tell me what page that is on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 9 in the B/C/S version, and 10 of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And page 12, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- of the English version.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at line 15 from the top. The sentence begins with, "I returned to Ovcara ..." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. That's toward the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please let me read this. I will read this part for you, and then I'll have a question. So this is what it says. This is part of your answer in response to the question of the presiding judge. "I returned to Ovcara, and when I returned to Ovcara I noticed already that they had pulled out of the 80th Brigade, members of the 80th Brigade, I see that they were the ones, the vehicles which were turned in the direction towards Negoslavci were now headed in the different direction, in the direction of Vukovar, and Captain Vezmarovic told me that he was withdrawing. This was not in contradiction. "Now, he had some version that he had been told -- that he had been informed of this by Lieutenant Karanfilov. I did not attend any conversation between them, but he told me that Lieutenant Karanfilov had told him even before I did to withdraw the unit." Have I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if you can see -- as you can see, this entire text is a bit -- is written in a bit -- in a funny or confused way, archaic. I think that some things that I may have just said there did not enter this transcript, and I think that between these two statements I -- in 2003 I had a conversation with Vezmarovic, and this is what I referred to in my statement. But -- but we did not discuss this in 1991. But this entire transcript is very poorly put together. It's full of mistakes, and very archaic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am interested in something else, Mr. Vukosavljevic. I am ending this part, and we're moving to something else. In the context of my earlier questions, and this is something to do with something you mentioned just now, that's to say he had some other version. Again, these words, the way you put them, also show that you seem to have some sort of doubts vis-a-vis his statement.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: You should take the audio recording of my statement. I believe that whoever was putting this on paper did it in a lopsided way, taking bits and pieces. I think you seem to be insisting on something that simply does not hold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukosavljevic, if I were tell you that this is a transcript of the audio recording which was typed out word for word, that's to say that your statement word for word the way you gave it before the trial chamber, was recorded here, and therefore I don't see that there is space for any doubt as to the accuracy of this transcript. You're saying that some words are scrambled up and so on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you do not know how I speak before a court of law. I always speak in an articulated way, I never leave my sentences unfinished. I always -- it's a narrative that I give, in the same way I have been giving one before this Tribunal. I believe that every person is entitled to taking his own approach to matters and I do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank the witness for answering my questions and I have no further questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to deal, if I may, with the exciting topic of command structure and the role of the security organ. You have told us and directed us to the rules or regulations that show that a security organ may politely advise a military unit about how to do things. It's in an advisory capacity. That is the principal role, is it not, for a security organ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would please notice, Mr. Moore is now asking you questions. Mr. Bulatovic is finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. Moore. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not a problem. May I deal with the topic of command structure and the role and function of the security organ. You have told us, and in cross-examination, that the function of a security organ is to, what I will say, is to perceive and advise, apart from their own role. Would that be correct, if one was dealing with, say, for example, military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The role of the military police is different, and there is a difference in the work of the military police and the organ of security. There is a bigger difference than that. The work of the military police is by and large a public work, whereas the security organ works in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect it's the way I put the question. You were referred to the security organ regulations, the role that they play within a military unit. And you seem to be suggesting that they had no command function with regard to other units. They could merely advise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. And this has been confirmed by the Defence counsel in their statements, and they even emphasised that particular role. And in that you agree with the Defence counsel, and I agree with you in what you have just put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we all agree, so that's splendid. Now, let's move on. That's the first part. The second part, how one deals -- the security organ deals with commands or orders, is where a security organ can convey an order. So he becomes - I will use the English word - he becomes the conduit pipe. He conveys the orders from, let us say, the commanding officer. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not the basic function of an organ of security. When the security organ visits different units, they can convey orders of the brigade commander to the battalion commander, and vice versa; they can convey information from the battalion commander to the brigade commander. As they move around, the security organs do receive information, can facilitate the exchange of that information, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I agree, thank you. But I would suggest there is a third way. That if, for example, we have a commanding officer of a unit or a brigade, is it not correct to say that he can, and I will use the word "empower" the security organ with the authority of the commanding officer? So he transfers the ability to command to the security organ for a specific task.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this doesn't happen that often. That doesn't happen often. In simple terms, the commanders do not yield their authority that easily. They do not pass their authority down to their subordinate officers. My commander, for example, never gave me any of his authorities, and not just the one -- the commander that we are talking about, but any commanders that I ever worked under. It doesn't happen that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you are not saying it can't happen and doesn't happen, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does happen, brigade commanders may transfer their authorities to one of their officers, but that is done in writing, it has to be done in writing, and if it is not done in writing, then it does not have any force, it does not mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the reality is that a commander or commanding officer can pass his authority down to a security organ to perform a specific task with the authority of the commanding officer residing in the security organ. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in hypothetical terms, in theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, let's move on, if I may, to, again, other exciting topics. Can I please refer you to the regulations on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY. It's Exhibit 396, and I would like, please, to ask you about Articles 20, but more particularly, Article 21. The page number, to assist the registry, is 0080-7699. Now, while that's being turned up, you have told us about going to the headquarters of the Guards Brigade where Mrksic was having a meeting. You then meet Vojnovic, you inform Vojnovic what is happening to Ovcara, and on your account, Vojnovic and yourself then return to speak to Mrksic and inform him of what is happening at Ovcara. So I just rehearse that to assist your recollection. What would you expect a commander to do, having been informed of such events occurring at Ovcara? What did you expect Mrksic to do, having been informed of that by people who were subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected him to take appropriate measures with a view to protection. However, the units that were at Ovcara that wanted to take over the prisoners of war, were under the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what would be the appropriate measures, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accommodation of the wounded in health facilities, health care facilities, and accommodation of the healthy ones in an appropriate way, in appropriate facilities, where they could tend to their normal needs and where they would be guarded until any further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you use the word "protection," what do you mean by that? Protection in respect of what? Commission of offences?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General protection, general protection of human beings, like the two of us are safe here at the Tribunal. Protection for prisoners of war who enjoy certain rights according to The Hague convention. For example, one-third of the meal that are normally received by the troops in units, the right to health care, the right to rest, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The right to be protected from physical attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The right to be protected from death?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. I'm not clear on his question. Is he actually using this witness as an expert witness or is he just confirming what the witness knows personally and what has already been the subject of examination-in-chief and cross-examination? I believe that my learned friend has changed the role of this witness, and he has transformed this witness into a person from which he seeks opinions on certain matters. And this is not the scope of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was prefaced, "What did you expect?" He is asking the witness's personal expectation. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I had actually concluded, but may I move on, then, please, to Article 21, as I have already referred to. I hope it's now found. It's, as I say, Exhibit 396.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have that document in front of you on the magic screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity of seeing this particular article, which is from the regulations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it in 1991, in 1999. I peruse it from time to time, and if there is a delicate situation, I always go back to it to consult this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why do you consult this document? Why do you peruse it? For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be informed. To be educated, to gain knowledge in order to avoid any mistakes or omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does this, or did this have an application, as far as your understanding, in 1991, either directly or indirectly at that time? I don't ask for a legal reply.

utterances.speaker: DRAGI VUKOSAVLJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw the title page of this law, I can see that it was printed in 1988, so it dates back to 1988, and I'm sure that it was applied in 1991, since it was out of print in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further re-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. You will be pleased to know that that is the end of the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance you have been able to give, and you are now free to return to your home and your affairs. Thank you, indeed. I would like to thank counsel and the staff - interpreters and transcript people - for extending the time today to enable this witness to conclude. The problems of securing a time when he could return were very considerable, and they have been able to be avoided. We will adjourn now and resume at noon on Monday.
